result.summary:
All findings below come from College Board's own properties — satsuite.collegeboard.org, bluebook.collegeboard.org, and the Fall 2026 SAT Suite of Assessments Proctor Manual PDF (satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/sats-proctor-manual.pdf), which I extracted and read directly. No recalled, leaked, or student-reported test content was searched for, visited, or used; nothing in this research touches actual questions, passages, or answers from any administration. The picture is consistent across sources: the digital SAT is a self-paced Bluebook exam where the app — not the proctor — times each student individually, students check in at 7:45 a.m. with doors closing at 8:00 a.m., testing starts around 8:15–8:30 a.m., and standard-time testers finish around 10:45–11:00 a.m. The single 10-minute break between Reading and Writing and Math is started and ended automatically by Bluebook; SAT Weekend students may leave the room during it without proctor dismissal, but may take only their snack and drink, and touching a phone at any point (including the break) is grounds for immediate dismissal and score cancellation.

Two areas deserve extra attention. First, device readiness is the highest-leverage controllable: Bluebook must be installed, "Test Your Device" run, and exam setup completed to generate the admission ticket — exam setup opens 5 days before test day. Requirements are now Windows 11 24H2 / macOS 15 / iPadOS 18 / ChromeOS 144 minimum, 3 hours of battery for SAT Suite, and 1 GB free (250 MB on iPad). Second, a mid-test crash or dead battery is recoverable and not catastrophic: answers are saved locally, the timer pauses for a limited period, and the student clicks Resume Testing and asks the proctor to click "Let Student Continue Testing" in Test Day Toolkit; device swap is a documented last resort. One genuine discrepancy exists in College Board's own documentation about the deadline to submit answers after an internet failure — the Testing Rules say 11:59 p.m. local time the next day, while the Bluebook answer-submission page says two days — so the safe reading is to submit the same day or, at worst, by 11:59 p.m. the following day. Scores for the Aug. 22, 2026 administration are scheduled for Sept. 4, 2026.

claims.claim: Required items on SAT test day
claims.detail: You MUST bring: (1) your fully charged testing device with Bluebook installed and exam setup already completed; (2) your up-to-date admission ticket from the Bluebook app (printed is preferred, electronic accepted); (3) an acceptable physical photo ID; (4) pencils or pens for scratch work; (5) your College Board username and password. Conditionally required: wired, non-Bluetooth headphones IF approved for text-to-speech or a screen reader. Epinephrine auto-injectors (EpiPens) are permitted with no accommodation request, but must be in a clear bag stored under the desk.

claims.claim: Optional items you may bring
claims.detail: A watch without an audible alarm (simple analog or non-smart digital only), a charging cable or portable charger/power bank, a bag or backpack, a drink and snacks (consumable only during scheduled breaks and in designated break areas), a backup testing device, an acceptable handheld calculator, and backup calculator or batteries. Per the Fall 2026 Proctor Manual, items allowed UNDER the desk are: power cord, portable charger, backup testing device, backup calculator or batteries, snack and drink, hand sanitizer/cleaning supplies. Bluebook also has an embedded Desmos calculator you can toggle between scientific and graphing at any point in the Math section, so a handheld calculator is genuinely optional.

claims.claim: Prohibited items — exhaustive list
claims.detail: Unless you have a College Board-approved accommodation, you cannot ACCESS these during the test OR breaks: phones, smartwatches, smart glasses or any eyewear providing internet/AI access, fitness trackers, other wearable technology, any electronic device other than your testing device (and backup); audio players, Bluetooth devices, wireless earbuds; detachable privacy screens; external keyboards for laptops or Chromebooks; stylus pens, Apple Pencils, smart pens; cameras, recording or listening devices; separate timers; notes, books, reference guides, papers, dictionaries; scratch paper not provided by the proctor; compasses, rulers, protractors, cutting devices; headphones, earbuds, or earplugs (unless required by an approved accommodation); prohibited calculator models. Weapons and firearms are strictly prohibited at test sites. Hats/head coverings may not be worn while testing except for medical or religious reasons; hoods must stay down.

claims.claim: Penalty for a prohibited device — this is the single highest-risk rule
claims.detail: College Board's exact framing: "If your prohibited electronic device makes noise or you're seen with it at any time, including during breaks, you may be dismissed immediately, your scores may be canceled, and the device may be confiscated." The Proctor Manual repeats this: "Accessing a prohibited device or having a device that makes any noise at any time, including breaks, is grounds for dismissal and possible confiscation of the electronic device as part of a thorough investigation." Test staff are instructed to collect and hold phones, or require students to store them in backpacks away from desks, including during breaks. Practical reading: the phone should be off and surrendered/stowed before check-in and not touched again until dismissal.

claims.claim: Acceptable photo ID — the five criteria
claims.detail: An acceptable ID must: (1) be a valid (unexpired) photo ID that is government-issued or issued by your school; (2) be an original, physical document — not photocopied and not electronic; digital IDs will NOT be accepted; (3) bear your full legal name exactly as it appears on your admission ticket; (4) show a recent, recognizable photograph that clearly matches your appearance on test day; (5) be in good condition with clearly legible English-language text.

claims.claim: Acceptable and unacceptable ID documents
claims.detail: ACCEPTABLE: government-issued driver's license or non-driver ID card (physical); official school student ID from your current school (physical); government-issued passport or U.S. Global Entry card; government-issued military or national ID card; SAT Student ID Form prepared by your school or a notary (homeschooled, U.S. only, under 21). NOT ACCEPTABLE: any digital/electronic ID; damaged (worn, torn, scuffed, scarred) documents; documents that appear tampered with or digitally altered; credit or debit cards; birth certificates; Social Security cards; employee IDs; temporary IDs; ChildFind cards; anything stating "not valid as identification." Test takers 21 or older must present an official government-issued photo ID — school IDs are no longer eligible at that age. Testing outside your home country generally requires a valid passport (with country-specific exceptions listed on the page for Ghana, Hong Kong, Nepal, Nigeria, India, Jordan, Korea, Thailand, UAE, Vietnam, Pakistan).

claims.claim: Admission ticket — generated only after exam setup, available 5 days out
claims.detail: The admission ticket comes from the Bluebook app itself, not from registration. Exam setup opens 5 days before test day: College Board emails instructions, you connect to the internet, close and reopen Bluebook so it updates, sign in, complete exam setup, and Bluebook then generates your admission ticket. Printed is preferred; electronic is accepted. The manual/site both note the ticket must be "up-to-date" — if test center information changes, reopen Bluebook to refresh it. Name on the ticket must match the ID exactly.

claims.claim: Device requirements — current minimums
claims.detail: Windows 11 version 24H2 minimum (Windows 10 is no longer supported for 2026-27); macOS 15 minimum; iPadOS 18 minimum; ChromeOS 144 minimum. Free storage: 1 GB on all devices except iPad, which needs 250 MB. Minimum battery life: 3 hours for SAT Suite (4 hours for AP). Chromebooks must be school-managed with verified mode enabled — Bluebook will not work otherwise. Mice are always allowed. External keyboards are permitted with tablets for certain exams but NEVER with laptops. You cannot test on a mobile phone. Virtual machines, thin clients, and remote environments are prohibited and "could result in disciplinary measures, including score cancellation."

claims.claim: Test-day-morning device checklist
claims.detail: On the morning of the test: connect to the internet; close and reopen Bluebook so it pulls the latest version; run "Test Your Device" to verify free space and readiness; sign in; check the homepage for last-minute messages and updated test center information; disable parental controls and content filters; charge the battery fully. Close all applications other than Bluebook before the test begins — running any other application during the test is a Testing Rules violation.

claims.claim: Charging and power during the test
claims.detail: Devices should arrive fully charged but may be plugged into available outlets. Per the Fall 2026 Proctor Manual: "The testing clock won't stop, so students should continue to test while their device charges." Allowed: being assigned an open seat near an outlet; proctors moving power strips, extension cords, or laptop carts; students using their own power banks WITHOUT permission (stored under the desk when not in use). Not allowed once testing has started: moving some students so others can charge, moving furniture, or replacing the battery on the testing device during testing. Proctors are told to watch for low-battery warnings during the break and tell students to plug in.

claims.claim: If the device dies or crashes mid-test — the test DOES resume
claims.detail: Per the Fall 2026 Proctor Manual: "If a technical issue during timed testing prevents a student from continuing, the timer will pause for a limited period, giving students a chance to recover. And, because answers are saved to the device, they can pick up where they left off." Fix order: (1) exit Bluebook, close background apps, sign in again; (2) restart the device and reopen Bluebook; (3) device swap to a backup device, only as a last resort. In all cases the proctor must open the student's profile in Test Day Toolkit and click "Let Student Continue Testing." The student clicks Resume Testing on their Bluebook homepage. On a device swap the student should be returned to the last question viewed; if returned to an earlier question they re-enter answers, unless more than 5 answers would need re-entry, in which case a retest irregularity is filed. Critical caveat: never swap devices after testing time runs out — answers could be lost, and answers must be submitted from the device you finish on. Note also: "Exiting the test, closing laptops, and covering tablets can lead to incomplete answer submission and delayed scores or retesting" — so do not close the lid at the break.

claims.claim: Reporting time vs. start time
claims.detail: Doors open / check-in begins at 7:45 a.m.; doors close at 8:00 a.m. unless your admission ticket says otherwise. You cannot be admitted once testing has started. Students borrowing a College Board-issued device must arrive 30 minutes early to sign in and complete exam setup. Room check-in takes roughly 15–30 minutes; testing typically begins between 8:15 and 8:30 a.m. Your seat is assigned, not chosen. You connect to test center Wi-Fi, open Bluebook, and enter a start code the proctor provides. The proctor answers procedure questions only — never questions about test content. Standard time ends around 10:45–11:00 a.m.; extended time around noon–12:15 p.m.; double time around 1:00–1:15 p.m. Late arrivals are sent to a late-testing room if one exists, otherwise to the test coordinator.

claims.claim: The 10-minute break — how it works mechanically
claims.detail: Standard timing gives exactly one 10-minute break, between the Reading and Writing section and the Math section (each section is about an hour, split into two separately timed modules). Bluebook — not the proctor — times the test and starts the break automatically, and displays break instructions. "Students can't start or end scheduled breaks early." When break time ends the student clicks a button to start the next section; no proctor action or instruction is needed. Because each student enters their own start code, start times and therefore break times are staggered across the room. Proctors do not time students or announce time remaining. Students approved for extended time on the whole test may receive a 20-minute nutrition break instead of the 10-minute break.

claims.claim: What you MAY and MAY NOT do during the break, and whether you can leave the room
claims.detail: You MAY leave the testing room during the scheduled break — "SAT Weekend students can leave the room without asking the proctor to dismiss them." You may take ONLY your snack and drink with you. You should keep your ID with you at all times. You may eat and drink during scheduled breaks and in designated break areas (snacks/drinks are otherwise off-limits during testing). You MAY NOT: access a phone or any other prohibited electronic device (immediate-dismissal offense); go to a locker at any time during the test or breaks; discuss test content with anyone; leave the room with anything other than your snack and drink. Leave your testing device OPEN — do not close the lid or cover the tablet, since that can cause incomplete answer submission. Proctors are explicitly instructed to watch for and report: excessive breaks, returning late from break, leaving the room with anything other than a snack, using the device for anything other than testing, accessing a phone, and talking to other students after a warning. Unscheduled breaks are permitted but you LOSE testing time — the clock keeps running (only students with an approved "breaks as needed" accommodation get a Pause button). Students who leave for an unscheduled break should take nothing with them.

claims.claim: You must stay for the full standard time and cannot submit early
claims.detail: Testing Rules: "You must stay for the full length of the standard time Test. You cannot submit your answers before the standard timer runs out." You also must not leave the testing room after finishing without being dismissed by staff. At the end, answers submit automatically; the proctor collects scratch paper, returns your items, and dismisses you silently because others may still be testing. (Only students with approved extended time may end a section after standard time has elapsed, by choice.)

claims.claim: Test security agreement — what you agree not to do with test content
claims.detail: You must acknowledge agreement to the Testing Rules before testing. Prohibited conduct explicitly includes: "copy or record Test questions, memorize questions for the purpose of writing them down later, or take a screenshot during the Test"; "discuss or share information about Test questions with others"; allowing others to see your questions or answers; using answer keys or receiving information from others about test content. Note that memorizing questions with intent to write them down later is itself named as a violation — this covers post-test online discussion of specific items, not just in-room cheating. Also prohibited: any attempt to gain an unfair advantage "including through cyber or digital methods, disabling test security features, or using unauthorized smart devices"; running applications other than Bluebook; accessing phones/mobile devices/internet resources during the test or breaks; using AI tools such as ChatGPT or Photomath; impersonation; switching devices or seats without permission; possessing answer keys, cheat sheets, or test content; testing twice in the same testing window without an approved retest.

claims.claim: Penalties for violating the test security agreement
claims.detail: Testing Rules state College Board may "deny you admission to the Test; remove you from the testing room; stop your Test; require you to use a College Board–issued testing device; decline to score your Test; withhold or cancel your official scores." For deliberate violations, College Board may also prohibit you "from taking future College Board tests including SAT, AP, or CLEP." For testing irregularities College Board "may cancel an entire test administration or individual registrations, decline to score all or part of the Test, not issue official scores, or cancel official scores." Practically: the penalties escalate from same-day dismissal to permanent bans from the entire College Board testing ecosystem, and they can be applied after the fact — score cancellation is not limited to what a proctor catches in the room.

claims.claim: Voluntary score cancellation by the student
claims.detail: You may cancel your own scores through your College Board account, but "your request must be submitted through your College Board account by no later than 11:59 p.m. ET 1 week after your Test date" for SAT Weekend. Once submitted, scores cannot be reinstated or reported to you or to any institution. Cancellation requests cannot be submitted by phone or email. (SAT School Day uses a different path — staff submit a student-requested cancellation form in Test Day Toolkit, within five days.)

claims.claim: If answers don't submit because of an internet problem
claims.detail: Testing Rules: "If your testing device is not connected to the internet when the Test ends and your answers are not submitted, you have until 11:59 p.m. local time the next day to reconnect to the internet and submit your answers." The Bluebook SAT Weekend answer-submission page instead states "You have until two days after the test to submit your answers," and describes the steps: open Bluebook on the SAME device used for testing, sign in, find your SAT under "Your Tests" (check the "Past" tab if it isn't visible), click "Submit Answers," and try a different network if it fails. That page adds that if answers remain unsubmitted, College Board will score the exam using the responses it collected during the session. NOTE: these two official pages disagree on the deadline — treat 11:59 p.m. local time the day after the test as the operative limit and submit the same evening if at all possible.

claims.claim: Technical problems during the test — what to do in the room
claims.detail: Raise your hand and tell the proctor; do not try to fix it silently and do not switch devices or seats on your own (switching without permission is itself a violation). Recovery is proctor-mediated through Test Day Toolkit. The timer pauses only for a limited period, so speed matters. If the issue can't be resolved at your seat you may be sent to a help room. For issues before you've entered the start code the sequence is: re-enter the start code, confirm you're marked present in Test Day Toolkit, restart the device and reopen Bluebook, then use a backup device. Test-center technical support lines: 866-630-9305 (U.S.) or +1-212-713-8000 (international).

claims.claim: How to get a makeup test
claims.detail: For SAT Weekend, you generally do not apply for a makeup — College Board contacts you. Makeups may be offered when "your test center is unable to open on test day" or when "a misadministration or irregularity occurs." If selected, you must bring an updated admission ticket, test only at the center for which you are registered or authorized, take only the tests you registered for on the original date, and complete the entire test at the makeup administration. If you believe a test-day problem affected you and no one has contacted you, contact Customer Service at sat.org/inquiry, 866-756-7346 (U.S.), or +1-212-713-7789 (international). In documented past incidents (e.g., the March 8, 2026 technical issue) College Board offered affected students a makeup where available, plus a refund and a voucher. For in-school administrations, retests are set up by the school via an Irregularity Report (IR) in Test Day Toolkit; retest-eligible scenarios include testing disruptions such as fire alarms, technical issues after testing started and before time ran out, becoming sick after testing started, and misadministrations. Scenarios that do NOT call for a retest include answer submission errors, absences, and rule violations. Each student gets only 2 retest opportunities due to irregularities, and when you retest you retake the entire assessment.

claims.claim: Score release timeline
claims.detail: "Most scores from weekend tests are released 2–4 weeks after test day," though the published schedule is tighter in practice. Published Fall 2026 SAT Weekend release dates: Aug. 22, 2026 → Sept. 4, 2026; Sept. 12, 2026 → Sept. 25, 2026; Oct. 3, 2026 → Oct. 16, 2026; Nov. 7, 2026 → Nov. 20, 2026; Dec. 5, 2026 → Dec. 18, 2026 (roughly 13 days each). Scores appear in an online score report in your College Board account at studentscores.collegeboard.org, most recent score at the top. Sending scores to colleges is a separate student-initiated action, and college-side processing times vary. If a retest IR was filed for you, your original score is held until the last published score release date.

claims.claim: Prohibited calculators (if bringing a handheld)
claims.detail: Prohibited: calculators with built-in CAS (Casio ClassPad 300/330/400, ClassPad II fx-CP400, ClassPad fx-CG 500/fx-CG500, Algebra fx 2.0, any model starting CFX-9970G; HP Prime, HP 48GII, any model starting 40G/49G/50G; TI-Nspire CAS, TI-Nspire CX II CAS, any model starting TI-89 or TI-92 or with "CAS" in the name — non-CAS TI-Nspire models ARE acceptable); calculators with apps/menus/programs performing symbolic algebra; QWERTY keyboards; wireless internet, Bluetooth, or cellular connectivity; built-in cameras or audio/video recording; tablets and laptops; electronic writing pads or pen-input devices; cell phone calculator apps; paper-tape calculators. Calculators can't have cords. Calculator covers and backup calculators/batteries stay under the desk. Before testing you must delete stored documents, turn off all sound, tape over infrared ports, and delete any programs with algebra functionality. 4-function calculators are permitted but not recommended.

claims.claim: Date-specific note for a test on Sunday, Aug. 23, 2026
claims.detail: Aug. 22, 2026 is a Saturday and a published SAT Weekend date with a Sept. 4, 2026 score release. Aug. 23, 2026 is the following Sunday; College Board runs Sunday administrations of the same test date for students who cannot test Saturday for religious observance. I did NOT find a College Board page confirming the score release date for the Sunday administration of that weekend specifically, nor confirming the Aug. 23 Sunday date itself — treat the Sunday date and its score release as UNVERIFIED and check the student's own admission ticket in Bluebook, which is the authoritative source for date, reporting time, and center.

claims.claim: Gaps I could not verify
claims.detail: UNVERIFIED: (1) There is no College Board page stating explicitly what happens if a battery fully dies with no charger available — the Bluebook help article on that question only covers prevention (3-hour battery for SAT Suite, arrive fully charged). The recoverable path documented in the Proctor Manual (timer pauses briefly, answers saved locally, Resume Testing + proctor authorization, device swap as last resort) is the closest official answer, but the length of the timer pause is stated only as "a limited period" and is never quantified. (2) Whether returning late from the 10-minute break costs testing time is not stated directly for scheduled breaks; only unscheduled breaks are explicitly said to cost time. (3) The exact time period after test day during which the confidentiality agreement binds you is not stated on the Testing Rules page — it is written as an unqualified prohibition. (4) College Board's own pages conflict on the post-test answer-submission deadline (next day 11:59 p.m. local vs. two days).

night_before_priorities: Open Bluebook tonight, sign in, run "Test Your Device," confirm exam setup is COMPLETE, and PRINT the admission ticket. Exam setup is what generates the ticket and it only opens 5 days out — if setup isn't done, nothing else on this list matters. Verify the name on the ticket matches the photo ID exactly.

Physically stage the bag tonight: printed admission ticket, physical photo ID (not digital — digital IDs are refused), pencils/pens, fully charged device, charging cable and/or power bank, watch with no alarm, snack and drink. Say the College Board username and password out loud to confirm you know them; you sign in on your own device at check-in.

Charge to 100% and confirm the OS meets the floor: Windows 11 24H2 / macOS 15 / iPadOS 18 / ChromeOS 144, with 1 GB free (250 MB on iPad) and at least 3 hours of battery. Do any OS or Bluebook update TONIGHT, never on test morning. Turn off parental controls and content filters.

Decide the phone plan now: powered off and handed to staff or stowed in the bag before check-in, not touched again until dismissal — including during the break. Being seen with it, or it making noise, at any time is grounds for immediate dismissal and score cancellation. Same for a smartwatch, smart glasses, fitness tracker, or earbuds; leave them home.

Internalize the timing: be at the center by 7:45 a.m., doors close at 8:00 a.m., no admission after testing starts. Add 30 minutes if borrowing a College Board device. Plan to be there until ~11:00 a.m. with standard time.

Know the break rules cold: one 10-minute break between Reading and Writing and Math, started and ended automatically by Bluebook, no early start or early end. You may leave the room without asking the proctor, but take ONLY your snack and drink, keep your ID on you, and leave your laptop OPEN — closing the lid can cause incomplete answer submission.

Memorize the crash protocol: raise your hand immediately, don't self-rescue. Answers are saved on the device and the timer pauses briefly; you'll click Resume Testing and the proctor clicks "Let Student Continue Testing." Never switch devices or seats without permission. Speed matters because the pause window is limited.

Do the morning ritual before leaving the house: connect to the internet, close and reopen Bluebook so it updates, sign in, and check the homepage for last-minute messages or a changed test center. Close every other application before testing begins — running anything besides Bluebook is a rules violation.

Commit to saying nothing about specific questions afterward, anywhere. Memorizing questions to write down later and discussing questions with others are both named violations, and penalties run from score cancellation to a permanent ban from SAT, AP, and CLEP. Walking out and posting about items is the one avoidable way to lose a good score after the fact.

Set the expectation for after: you must stay for the full standard time and cannot submit early. If the internet drops at the end and answers don't submit, reopen Bluebook on the SAME device and submit by 11:59 p.m. local the next day. Scores for the Aug. 22, 2026 date release Sept. 4, 2026; self-cancellation, if ever wanted, is due 11:59 p.m. ET one week after test day and is irreversible.

result.summary:
The Digital SAT's published structure is unchanged as of August 2026. I verified directly against the live Assessment Framework PDF (downloaded and text-extracted rather than trusting a summary), the 2026-27 SAT Weekend Student Guide PDF, and the satsuite.collegeboard.org structure, dates, rules, ID, calculator, Sunday-testing, and score-release pages. The test remains a two-stage multistage-adaptive (MST) design: two sections (Reading and Writing, Math), each delivered as two separately timed modules, where performance on module 1 routes the student to an easier or harder module 2. Reading and Writing is 2 x 32 minutes with 27 questions per module (25 operational + 2 pretest) for 54 total; Math is 2 x 35 minutes with 22 questions per module (20 operational + 2 pretest) for 44 total. That is 98 questions, 90 of them scored, in 134 minutes (2 hours 14 minutes) of testing time, plus a 10-minute break between sections. Scoring is unchanged: 200-800 per section, 400-1600 total.

No Assessment Framework edition newer than v3.01 (August 2024) exists. The PDF served at the canonical College Board URL today still reads "Assessment Framework for the Digital SAT Suite, Version 3.01, August 2024" on its title page and in its own suggested citation, and no v3.02 or v4 surfaces anywhere. The 2026-27 changes are operational, not structural: Bluebook now requires Windows 11 and ChromeOS 144+, Chromebooks need verified mode, the embedded Desmos calculator is resizable, reference sheets have alternate layouts, and charts/images support zoom and pan; a registration Waitlist launched in the U.S. for fall 2026; Text-to-Speech (Embedded) students can now test at any weekend center; and students needing text-to-speech or a screen reader must bring their own wired, non-Bluetooth headphones. Timing note: August 22, 2026 IS the August administration (today), its scores release September 4, 2026, and its Sunday religious-observance alternate is tomorrow, August 23, 2026. One trap worth flagging: Sunday alternates are NOT always the next day — September's is the 20th (not the 13th) and October's is the 18th (not the 4th), because the adjacent Sundays fall on religious holidays.

claims.claim: The two-stage multistage-adaptive (MST) design is still current and is the official model
claims.detail: Assessment Framework v3.01 states College Board 'employs a simple two-stage MST model' for the digital SAT Suite, depicted in Figure 1. Stage 1 gives 'a broad mix of easy, medium-difficulty, and hard questions'; stage 2 gives 'a targeted mix of questions' based on stage-1 performance. Each section is routed independently. The 2026-27 Student Guide repeats this: 'The SAT, and all tests in the SAT Suite of Assessments, uses multistage adaptive testing.' The set of module 1 + module 2 is officially called a 'panel'. Within a module, students can navigate freely — preview upcoming questions, flag and return to earlier ones — but cannot return to module 1 after it is submitted.

claims.claim: Exact structure: 2 sections, 4 modules, 98 questions, 134 minutes, 10-minute break
claims.detail: Reading and Writing: one section, two separately timed modules, 32 minutes each = 64 minutes; 54 questions total. Math: one section, two separately timed modules, 35 minutes each = 70 minutes; 44 questions total. Total testing time 2 hours 14 minutes (134 minutes) for 98 questions. A 10-minute break separates the Reading and Writing section from the Math section. Framework-published average time per question: Math 1.59 minutes; Reading and Writing works out to ~1.19 minutes. Most questions are multiple choice; some Math questions are student-produced response (type-in) rather than select.

claims.claim: Pretest (unscored) questions: exactly 2 per module, 8 per test
claims.detail: Verbatim from Framework v3.01 tables: Reading and Writing — '1st module: 25 operational questions and 2 pretest questions / 2nd module: 25 operational questions and 2 pretest questions / Total: 54 questions.' Math — '1st module: 20 operational questions and 2 pretest questions / 2nd module: 20 operational questions and 2 pretest questions / Total: 44 questions.' So 90 operational + 8 pretest = 98. Crucially, pretest items are indistinguishable from scored ones by design: the Framework says this 'ensures that students give maximum attention and effort to these questions.' Practical consequence for a student — you cannot identify or skip them, so treat every question as scored. They also explain why an occasional question feels off-pattern or oddly hard: it may simply be a trial item that counts for nothing.

claims.claim: Score scale unchanged: 200-800 per section, 400-1600 total
claims.detail: The 2026-27 SAT Weekend Student Guide states: 'The SAT is scored on a 400-1600 point scale,' with section scores of 200-800 for Reading and Writing and 200-800 for Math, total score being the sum of the two. Framework v3.01 Figure 2 (Digital SAT Suite Vertical Scale) confirms SAT 400-1600, alongside PSAT 10 and PSAT/NMSQT at 320-1520 and PSAT 8/9 at 240-1440 on a common vertical scale.

claims.claim: NO Assessment Framework newer than v3.01 (August 2024) has been published
claims.detail: I fetched the live PDF at the canonical URL on 2026-08-22 and extracted its text. The title page reads 'Assessment Framework for the Digital SAT Suite — Version 3.01, August 2024' and the document's own suggested citation reads: 'College Board. 2024. Assessment Framework for the Digital SAT Suite, version 3.01 (August 2024). New York: College Board.' The v3.01 changelog describes only minor corrections (notably restoring 'information inadvertently left off of the reproduction of the reference sheet of common math formulas') plus updates reflecting the completed transition to digital. Targeted searches for v3.02 or v4 return nothing. CONCLUSION: v3.01 is still the governing content/skills specification, now two years old, and nothing about test content domains has changed since.

claims.claim: Official 2026-27 SAT weekend test dates and deadlines
claims.detail: Test date / registration deadline / change-cancel deadline: Aug 22 2026 / Aug 7 / Aug 11 — Sept 12 2026 / Aug 28 / Sept 1 — Oct 3 2026 / Sept 18 / Sept 22 — Nov 7 2026 / Oct 23 / Oct 27 — Dec 5 2026 / Nov 20 / Nov 24 — Mar 6 2027 / Feb 19 / Feb 23 — May 1 2027 / Apr 16 / Apr 20 — June 5 2027 / May 21 / May 25. Deadlines expire 11:59 p.m. ET. Late registration available worldwide for a fee. Students who need to borrow a device must register at least 30 days before the test date. In-school windows: Fall 2026 Oct 1-30; Spring 2027 Mar 1-Apr 30. NOTE: there is no January, February, or April weekend SAT.

claims.claim: The August 2026 administration is Saturday August 22, 2026 — which is TODAY — and its Sunday alternate is August 23, 2026
claims.detail: The August 2026 SAT was administered Saturday, August 22, 2026 (registration closed Aug 7; changes closed Aug 11). Its religious-observance Sunday alternate is Sunday, August 23, 2026. Scores for the Aug 22 administration release September 4, 2026. Anyone asking about 'the August test' as an upcoming event is either referring to the Sunday alternate tomorrow or has the cycle wrong — the Saturday sitting has already happened.

claims.claim: Full 2026-27 Sunday alternate date list — and two of them are NOT the day after the Saturday
claims.detail: Published Sunday dates: Aug 23 2026, Sept 20 2026, Oct 18 2026, Nov 8 2026, Dec 6 2026, Mar 7 2027, May 2 2027, June 6 2027. College Board's rule: 'Sunday tests are the day after each Saturday test date unless that Sunday is a religious holiday.' Apply that and two dates break the pattern and are easy to get wrong: the September Sunday is the 20th, NOT Sept 13 (eight days after the Sept 12 Saturday), and the October Sunday is the 18th, NOT Oct 4 (fifteen days after the Oct 3 Saturday) — both shifted because the adjacent Sundays fall on Jewish High Holy Days. A student who assumes 'Sunday = Saturday + 1' will show up on the wrong day or miscalculate prep time by up to two weeks. Always read the date printed on the admission ticket.

claims.claim: Sunday testing: eligibility, documentation, and process
claims.detail: Sunday administration is available ONLY to students who cannot test Saturday for religious reasons. Required documentation: a letter from an official religious leader that explains the religious reason, bears the official's signature, and is on letterhead from the religious or educational organization. Process: register, then contact SAT support via the SAT Student and Parent Inquiry Form selecting topic 'Registration' and detail 'Change Saturday/Sunday status'; once approved, print the admission ticket showing the Sunday date. Restrictions: you may take a given administration on Saturday OR Sunday, never both; Sunday testing is not available in India or Pakistan.

claims.claim: Whether the Sunday form is the same test form as Saturday is NOT published by College Board — UNVERIFIED
claims.detail: UNVERIFIED. I checked the Sunday testing page, both Sunday help-center articles, the testing rules, and the 2026-27 Student Guide. College Board publishes eligibility, documentation, dates, and the Saturday-or-Sunday-not-both restriction, but makes no public statement about whether the Sunday administration uses the identical form, a different form, or a form drawn from the same pool. Do not assert either way. What IS officially established and is what actually matters to a student: every published rule, the structure, timing, module counts, adaptive routing, scoring scale, calculator policy, ID policy, and score-release date are identical for Sunday testers. Sunday is a scheduling accommodation, not a different exam product, and there is no published basis for claiming it is harder, easier, or scored differently. Treat any claim about specific Sunday form identity from forums or prep marketing as unsourced.

claims.claim: Score release: 2-4 weeks typical; specific fall 2026 dates published
claims.detail: 'Most scores from weekend tests are released 2-4 weeks after test day.' Published fall 2026 release dates: Aug 22 test → Sept 4 2026; Sept 12 → Sept 25; Oct 3 → Oct 16; Nov 7 → Nov 20; Dec 5 → Dec 18. In practice this is roughly a 13-day turnaround, faster than the stated 2-4 week window. Scores appear in a detailed online score report in the student's College Board account; students choose which scores to send to colleges, and colleges' own processing timelines vary.

claims.claim: Bluebook and device changes for 2026-27
claims.detail: Bluebook now requires Windows 11 (Microsoft ended Windows 10 support) and raised the ChromeOS minimum to version 144. Bluebook runs on Chromebooks only when verified mode is enabled. New student-facing features: the embedded Math calculator is resizable; reference sheets can be viewed in a different layout; students can zoom and pan to inspect charts, graphs, and images. A registration Waitlist launched (U.S. only, fall 2026) to auto-place students if a seat opens at a full date/center. Educators can now sign in to Bluebook with a professional account and take full-length practice tests. Staff-side, Test Day Live gives a dashboard view of student progress across rooms. Bluebook must be downloaded and exam setup completed BEFORE test day — completing setup is what generates the admission ticket. You cannot test on a mobile phone.

claims.claim: Calculator policy: built-in Desmos plus approved bring-your-own, Math section only
claims.detail: Bluebook includes an embedded Desmos calculator that toggles between graphing and scientific modes, available for the entire Math section (both modules). Students may also bring an approved calculator: non-CAS graphing, scientific, or four-function. Prohibited: anything with CAS (computer algebra system) — including TI-Nspire CAS, HP Prime, and certain Casio ClassPad models — plus QWERTY keyboards, symbolic algebra manipulation, wireless/Bluetooth/cellular connectivity, built-in cameras or recorders, tablets, laptops, phone calculator apps, and electronic writing pads. Calculators are permitted ONLY during Math; during Reading and Writing the calculator must be under the desk. Students are asked to clear all saved formulas from a brought calculator before testing.

claims.claim: ID requirements — digital IDs are NOT accepted
claims.detail: Acceptable: government-issued driver's license or non-driver ID card, official school-produced student ID from your current school, government-issued passport or U.S. Global Entry card, government-issued military or national ID, or the SAT Student ID Form (school- or notary-prepared; U.S. centers only, under 21). Students 21+ may use only government-issued photo ID — student IDs are not accepted. NOT acceptable: digital or electronic IDs on a device, damaged/worn/torn documents, anything appearing tampered with, credit or debit cards even with a photo, birth certificates, Social Security cards, employee IDs, temporary ID cards. Every ID must be valid and unexpired, an original physical document, bear your full legal name exactly as on the admission ticket, and show a recent recognizable photo. A prior-year school ID stays valid through December 31 of the current calendar year. Testing staff may deny admission for discrepancies between ID and admission ticket.

claims.claim: What to bring and what is banned on test day
claims.detail: Bring: your approved testing device (laptop or tablet, never a phone) with Bluebook installed and exam setup complete, power cord and/or portable charger, admission ticket (printed or electronic), acceptable physical photo ID, pen or pencil for scratch work, and optionally an approved calculator, external mouse and mouse pad. Banned: phones, smartwatches, fitness trackers, headphones (except approved wired non-Bluetooth ones for text-to-speech/screen-reader accommodations), other wearables, books, reference guides, notes, compasses, protractors, dictionaries, highlighters, colored pencils, and detachable privacy screens. Close all applications other than Bluebook before the test begins. Students borrowing a College Board device must arrive 30 minutes early to complete setup and get their admission ticket. The SAT Testing Rules page was last revised May 19, 2026.

claims.claim: Published content domains and operational question distribution — Reading and Writing
claims.detail: Four domains, fixed proportions of the 50 operational RW questions. Information and Ideas — ~26% (12-14 questions); skills: Central Ideas and Details, Command of Evidence (Textual and Quantitative), Inferences. Craft and Structure — ~28% (13-15 questions); skills: Words in Context, Text Structure and Purpose, Cross-Text Connections. Expression of Ideas — ~20% (8-12 questions); skills: Rhetorical Synthesis, Transitions. Standard English Conventions — ~26% (11-15 questions); skills: Boundaries, Form/Structure/Sense. Within each module, questions appear grouped by domain in a fixed sequence (Information and Ideas, Craft and Structure, Expression of Ideas, Standard English Conventions), and within each domain except Standard English Conventions they are ordered easiest to hardest. That ordering is a legitimate, published pacing cue: difficulty resets at each domain boundary, so a hard question does not mean the rest of the module is hard.

claims.claim: Published content domains and operational question distribution — Math
claims.detail: Four domains across the 40 operational Math questions. Algebra — 13-15 questions; linear equations in one and two variables, linear functions, systems of two linear equations, linear inequalities. Advanced Math — 13-15 questions; equivalent expressions, nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables, nonlinear functions. Problem-Solving and Data Analysis — 5-7 questions; ratios/rates/proportions/units, percentages, one- and two-variable data, distributions and measures of center and spread, models and scatterplots, probability and conditional probability, inference from sample statistics and margin of error, evaluating statistical claims from observational studies and experiments. Geometry and Trigonometry — 5-7 questions; area and volume, lines/angles/triangles, right triangles and trigonometry, circles. Note the weighting: Algebra plus Advanced Math is roughly 65-75% of Math, so linear and nonlinear equation fluency dominates the section.

claims.claim: Why the adaptive design should not change test-taking behavior
claims.detail: Framework v3.01 states that the design 'is fair to all students and that students are best served by answering each digital SAT Suite test question to the best of their ability.' Two legitimate strategic implications follow from published facts, with no reliance on leaked content. First, because module 2 difficulty is set by module 1 performance and pretest items are invisible, there is no gameable pattern — every question in module 1 carries routing weight in addition to its own score contribution. Second, because students can navigate freely within a module and flag questions to revisit, and because difficulty restarts at each domain boundary in Reading and Writing, skipping a stuck question and returning is strictly better than burning time in sequence. There is no wrong-answer penalty, so leaving anything blank is never correct.

night_before_priorities: Confirm the exact date on your admission ticket, not from memory. Sunday alternates are NOT reliably 'the Saturday plus one' — Aug 23 and Nov 8 and Dec 6 are, but September's is the 20th (not the 13th) and October's is the 18th (not the 4th). The ticket is authoritative; print or save it tonight along with the reporting time and center address.

Get the device fully ready tonight: Bluebook installed and updated, exam setup completed (this is what generates the admission ticket), device charged to 100%, power cord and/or a portable charger packed. Verify OS compatibility now, not in the morning — Bluebook requires Windows 11 and ChromeOS 144+, and Chromebooks need verified mode. You cannot test on a phone.

Lay out an acceptable PHYSICAL photo ID — digital and phone-wallet IDs are rejected outright. It must be unexpired, undamaged, an original, and carry your full legal name exactly as printed on the admission ticket. A name mismatch or a worn card can get you turned away at the door.

Pack the calculator correctly if you bring one: non-CAS only, formulas cleared before test day, and remember it is allowed only during Math and must go under your desk during Reading and Writing. Bluebook's built-in Desmos (graphing and scientific, now resizable) is available for the whole Math section, so a brought calculator is optional insurance, not a requirement.

Internalize the pacing math instead of studying new content: 32 minutes for 27 Reading and Writing questions (about 1.2 min each) and 35 minutes for 22 Math questions (about 1.6 min each), per module. Decide tonight on a rule — for example, flag and move on at 90 seconds — because free navigation within a module makes skipping and returning strictly better than grinding in order.

Know that 8 of the 98 questions are unscored pretest items you cannot identify, and that there is no wrong-answer penalty. Together those mean: never leave a blank, and never let one bizarre-feeling question rattle you — it may literally count for nothing.

Use the Reading and Writing question order as a built-in pacing signal: questions are grouped by domain (Information and Ideas, then Craft and Structure, then Expression of Ideas, then Standard English Conventions) and run easy-to-hard within each domain, so difficulty resets at every domain boundary. Hitting a hard one does not mean the rest of the module is hard.

Do not cram new material. The governing content specification is still Assessment Framework v3.01 from August 2024 — nothing has changed in two years, so anything you have not learned by tonight will not move your score. Sleep is the higher-yield investment.
Set expectations for afterward: scores post 2-4 weeks out, in practice about 13 days. A Sunday Aug 23 sitting, like the Aug 22 Saturday, releases Sept 4, 2026.

Ignore any online chatter about 'what was on' a recent form or whether Sunday forms differ. College Board publishes nothing about Sunday form identity, so every such claim is unsourced — and seeking out recalled items is a test-security violation that can void your scores. Every published rule, timing, structure, and scoring detail is identical for Sunday testers.

result.summary:
I verified the Digital SAT Math taxonomy directly against four primary College Board documents rather than prep-site paraphrases: the *Digital SAT Suite Specifications Overview* (Table 3), the full *Assessment Framework for the Digital SAT Suite* (Tables 19, 20, 21–24), *Skills Insight for the Digital SAT Suite* (score-band skill statements), and the official *Bluebook Test Directions* PDF (the verbatim SPR rules plus the acceptable/unacceptable examples table). The structure is fixed and public: 44 questions (40 operational + 4 embedded pretest) in two 35-minute adaptive modules of 22, ~1.59 min/question, Desmos graphing calculator and reference sheet available throughout, ~75% multiple-choice and ~25% student-produced response, ~30% of questions set in context, and questions arranged easiest-to-hardest *within* each module. Domain weights for the SAT are Algebra ≈35% / 13–15 q, Advanced Math ≈35% / 13–15 q, Problem-Solving & Data Analysis ≈15% / 5–7 q, Geometry & Trigonometry ≈15% / 5–7 q — counted against the 40 operational questions. There are exactly 19 named skill/knowledge testing points (5 / 3 / 7 / 4 across the four domains), and Table 20 additionally publishes the MC-vs-SPR split per domain, which is the piece almost no prep site reports.

The most decision-relevant finding is a structural asymmetry nobody states outright: Advanced Math packs 13–15 questions into only 3 testing points (~4–5 questions each), while Problem-Solving & Data Analysis spreads 5–7 questions across 7 testing points (~0–1 question each). So "Nonlinear functions" is roughly five times denser per unit of study than "Evaluating statistical claims." For the 600–750 band specifically, I did not have to speculate: College Board's own Skills Insight anchors band 6 at 610–670 and band 7 at 680–800 and publishes exactly which skills separate them — number-of-solutions conditions, translations of functions, solving a complex formula for a variable of interest, finding an unknown *constant* in a nonlinear equation, representations containing *variable constants*, circles (arc length/sectors/tangents), sine–cosine complementary angles, degree↔radian conversion, scale-factor effects, and how mean/median/range shift when a data set changes. That band-anchored list is the highest-quality difficulty evidence available and it is official, not reputational. The SPR rules are the single cheapest point source: the official examples table shows 0.66 and 0.67 are *rejected* for an answer of 2/3 while .6666, .6667, 0.666, and 0.667 are accepted — a pure formatting rule that can silently cost a student several of the ~11 SPR questions.

claims.claim: The Math section is 44 questions in two adaptive 35-minute modules; only 40 are scored
claims.detail: Official Table 1 and Framework §4.1.2: the Math section consists of 44 questions divided into two equal modules of 22. Of each module's 22 questions, 20 are operational (scored) and 2 are embedded pretest (unscored, indistinguishable from real ones). Total time 70 minutes, 35 minutes per module. Framework §4.1.4 states students have on average 1.59 minutes per question. All published domain question counts (13-15, 5-7, etc.) are counted against the 40 OPERATIONAL questions, not 44 — this is why prep sites that scale percentages against 44 report inflated counts.

claims.claim: Four domains with official weights and question counts (SAT, Table 3 / Table 19)
claims.detail: Algebra ≈35% / 13–15 questions. Advanced Math ≈35% / 13–15 questions. Problem-Solving and Data Analysis ≈15% / 5–7 questions. Geometry and Trigonometry ≈15% / 5–7 questions. Verbatim from Table 3 of the Specifications Overview and confirmed independently in Table 19 of the Assessment Framework. Note: PSAT/NMSQT and PSAT 10 differ (Advanced Math ≈32.5%/12–14, PSDA ≈20%/7–9, Geo&Trig ≈12.5%/4–6), so do not mix PSAT figures into SAT planning. Also SAT-only: circles are assessed ONLY on the SAT within Geometry and Trigonometry.

claims.claim: Algebra domain — the 5 official skill/knowledge testing points
claims.detail: Verbatim from Table 3 / Table 21: (1) Linear equations in one variable; (2) Linear equations in two variables; (3) Linear functions; (4) Systems of two linear equations in two variables; (5) Linear inequalities in one or two variables. Domain claim: 'Students will interpret, create, use, represent, and solve problems using linear representations; and make connections between different representations of linear relationships.'

claims.claim: Advanced Math domain — only 3 official testing points carry 13–15 questions
claims.detail: Verbatim from Table 3 / Table 22: (1) Equivalent expressions; (2) Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables; (3) Nonlinear functions. Domain claim covers 'absolute value, quadratic, exponential, polynomial, rational, radical, and other nonlinear equations,' plus interpreting, rewriting, making strategic use of structure, and connecting different representations of a nonlinear relationship. This is the highest-density block on the test: 3 labels, 13–15 questions.

claims.claim: Problem-Solving & Data Analysis — 7 official testing points share only 5–7 questions
claims.detail: Verbatim from Table 3 / Table 23 (SAT list): (1) Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units; (2) Percentages; (3) One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread; (4) Two-variable data: models and scatterplots; (5) Probability and conditional probability; (6) Inference from sample statistics and margin of error; (7) Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments. Note testing points 6 and 7 are SAT-only — the PSAT lists drop 'Evaluating statistical claims.' With 7 labels and 5–7 questions, several of these testing points can be entirely absent from any given form.

claims.claim: Geometry & Trigonometry — 4 official testing points, 5–7 questions
claims.detail: Verbatim from Table 3 / Table 24 (SAT list): (1) Area and volume; (2) Lines, angles, and triangles; (3) Right triangles and trigonometry; (4) Circles. The SAT domain claim explicitly names: length/area/volume and scale factors; congruence, similarity and sufficiency via vertical angles, triangles, and parallel lines cut by a transversal; the Pythagorean theorem, right-triangle AND unit-circle trigonometry, and special right triangles; and properties/theorems relating to circles. Circles is the only testing point in the entire Math section assessed on the SAT but on no other test in the suite.

claims.claim: Table 20: the MC vs SPR split BY DOMAIN — grid-ins are concentrated in Algebra and Advanced Math
claims.detail: Assessment Framework Table 20, SAT row: Algebra MC 10–11 / SPR 3–4. Advanced Math MC 10–11 / SPR 3–4. Problem-Solving and Data Analysis MC 4–5 / SPR 1–2. Geometry and Trigonometry MC 4–5 / SPR 1–2. Totals: MC 28–32, SPR 8–12. Practical consequence: 6–8 of the ~8–12 grid-ins come from Algebra + Advanced Math, so SPR entry-format errors disproportionately destroy points in the two heaviest domains. This table is published by College Board and is almost never cited by prep sites.

claims.claim: ~75% multiple choice / ~25% SPR; SPR questions can have more than one correct answer
claims.detail: Framework §2.3.8 and §4.1.6: approximately 75 percent of Math questions use the four-option multiple-choice format; the remainder are student-produced response. Table 19 quantifies this as MC ≈75% / 28–32 questions and SPR ≈25% / 8–12 questions of the 40 operational. Critically, §4.1.6 states Math SPR questions 'may have more than one answer that students could enter and have counted correct, although they are directed to provide only one answer per question' — i.e. an unreduced fraction or an equivalent decimal is fine, and a student who gets a valid alternate form should not second-guess it. Princeton Review independently estimates ~11 of 44 questions are SPR.

claims.claim: OFFICIAL SPR ENTRY RULES — verbatim from the Bluebook test directions
claims.detail: Verbatim bullets: (1) 'If you find more than one correct answer, enter only one answer.' (2) 'You can enter up to 5 characters for a positive answer and up to 6 characters (including the negative sign) for a negative answer.' (3) 'If your answer is a fraction that doesn't fit in the provided space, enter the decimal equivalent.' (4) 'If your answer is a decimal that doesn't fit in the provided space, enter it by truncating or rounding at the fourth digit.' (5) 'If your answer is a mixed number (such as 3½), enter it as an improper fraction (7/2) or its decimal equivalent (3.5).' (6) 'Don't enter symbols such as a percent sign, comma, or dollar sign.' The paper-accommodation version adds: 'but no more,' and requires circling exactly one answer.

claims.claim: OFFICIAL SPR EXAMPLES TABLE — what is rejected (this is the highest-value 5 minutes on the list)
claims.detail: The directions print an 'Acceptable ways to enter answer' vs 'Unacceptable: will NOT receive credit' table. Answer 3.5 → ACCEPTED: 3.5, 3.50, 7/2. REJECTED: 31/2, 3 1/2. Answer 2/3 → ACCEPTED: 2/3, .6666, .6667, 0.666, 0.667. REJECTED: 0.66, .66, 0.67, .67. Answer −1/3 → ACCEPTED: −1/3, −.3333, −0.333. REJECTED: −.33, −0.33. The operative rule: for a repeating decimal you must FILL the available space — two decimal places is rejected even though it rounds correctly. Trailing zeros are fine (3.50), unreduced/alternate forms are fine (7/2 for 3.5), a leading zero is optional (.6666 and 0.666 both work). Mixed numbers are the classic silent zero.

claims.claim: The character count includes the decimal point, the fraction bar, and the negative sign
claims.detail: Not stated as a rule but forced by the official examples: '.6666' is accepted at exactly 5 characters (period + 4 digits), '0.666' is 5 characters, '−0.333' is 6 characters, and '−.3333' is 6 characters. So the field is 5 glyphs positive / 6 glyphs negative counting every symbol, not 5 significant digits. Practical read: a negative answer buys you exactly one extra character, spent on the minus sign, so drop the leading zero (−.3333 beats −0.333 for precision).

claims.claim: Skills Insight defines the 600–750 band precisely: band 6 = 610–670, band 7 = 680–800
claims.detail: Table 3 / Table 15 of Skills Insight: Math performance score bands are 1 (<370), 2 (370–410), 3 (420–460), 4 (470–540), 5 (550–600), 6 (610–670), 7 (680–800). Band 6 begins at the SAT 75th percentile; band 7 begins at the SAT 90th percentile. A student in the 600–750 range straddles the top of band 5 through band 7, so the band 6 and band 7 skill statements ARE the official answer to 'what separates this student from 800.' This is the strongest available difficulty evidence and it is primary-source, not reputational.

claims.claim: OFFICIAL band 6 (610–670) discriminating skills — the first wall
claims.detail: Algebra: interpret intercepts/slope for COMPLEX linear equations in real-world context; interpret the meaning of a given value in a complex linear function; connect table ↔ algebraic form ↔ graph ↔ solution; and 'find the number of solutions to a multistep linear equation; find the number of solutions to a system of two linear equations, or determine a possible second equation in a system with no, exactly one, or infinitely many solutions.' Advanced Math: create a quadratic or exponential equation from context and solve for an unknown; interpret a key feature of an exponential/quadratic graph in context; connect algebraic form to graph, and 'understand how a translation of a function affects the key features of the graph or the equation.' PSDA: multistep ratios/rates/percentages and DERIVED units (products and quotients); average rate of change from a graph; compare distributions by center and spread and 'the effect of outliers on mean and median'; conditional probability including two-way tables. Geo/Trig: multistep Pythagorean; triangle angle sum; congruence/similarity of right triangles including trig ratios; 'identifying the impact of changes by a scale factor on perimeter, area, and/or volume.'

claims.claim: OFFICIAL band 7 (680–800) discriminating skills — the ceiling skills
claims.detail: Algebra: connect representations of linear equations/functions/systems/inequalities 'when these representations include symbolic representations that may contain VARIABLE CONSTANTS'; create/solve a linear equation or system, or 'identify the correct coefficients or constants in the equation(s) that represent(s) the situation.' Advanced Math: 'Solve a complex equation or formula for a variable of interest'; use properties of exponents and of polynomial, rational, and radical expressions to rewrite complex expressions USING STRUCTURE, or determine the most suitable form of an equation to display a certain feature; 'Solve problems with or without context involving one or more nonlinear equations in order to find the value of an UNKNOWN CONSTANT.' PSDA: determine how mean, median, and range are AFFECTED BY CHANGES in the data set and compare two data sets; 'Identify or describe the POPULATION to which the results of a research study can reasonably be extended.' Geo/Trig: missing values in 2D/3D solids via area, surface area, or volume; 'properties and theorems related to circles and parts of circles, such as radii, diameters, tangents, angles, arcs, ARC LENGTH, and SECTORS'; 'the relationship between SINE AND COSINE OF COMPLEMENTARY ANGLES; convert between degree measure and RADIAN measure.'

claims.claim: DERIVED frequency per testing point: Advanced Math points are ~5x denser than PSDA points
claims.detail: College Board publishes question counts per DOMAIN but never per testing point. Dividing published counts by published testing-point counts gives the expected density: Advanced Math 13–15 q / 3 points ≈ 4–5 questions per point. Algebra 13–15 q / 5 points ≈ 3 questions per point. Geometry & Trigonometry 5–7 q / 4 points ≈ 1–2 questions per point. Problem-Solving & Data Analysis 5–7 q / 7 points ≈ 0–1 question per point. Consequence: 'Nonlinear functions' and 'Equivalent expressions' are each worth several times more raw points than 'Evaluating statistical claims' or 'Inference from sample statistics and margin of error,' which may not appear at all on a given form. This is arithmetic on official numbers, not a published College Board statistic — treat the per-point numbers as an expectation, not a guarantee, since College Board does not commit to uniform distribution within a domain.

claims.claim: Questions are arranged easiest-to-hardest WITHIN each module, and module 1 determines which module 2 you get
claims.detail: Framework §4.1.1 and the Specifications Overview: 'Across each module, questions are arranged from easiest to hardest.' The first (routing) module is a broad mix of easy/medium/hard; the second module's average difficulty is targeted to performance on the first. Once Bluebook advances a student to module 2 they may NOT return to module 1. Embedded pretest questions 'appear in differing locations throughout the sequence,' so a jarringly hard early question may simply be unscored. Strategic read for a 600–750 student: module 1 accuracy sets the score ceiling, and the cheapest questions on the whole test are the first several of each module.

claims.claim: Desmos graphing calculator and the reference sheet are available for the ENTIRE Math section
claims.detail: Specifications Overview: 'Calculator: A built-in graphing calculator is available on the entire Math section. (Students can also bring their own approved calculator.)' and 'Reference sheet: On the Math section, students have access to a list of common formulas.' There is no no-calculator module on the digital SAT. Princeton Review notes the built-in tool is a version of Desmos and calls learning to leverage it 'key to improving your digital SAT score.'

claims.claim: Exact contents of the provided reference sheet — so you know what NOT to memorize
claims.detail: The official Bluebook directions reference sheet provides: A = lw, V = lwh, A = ½bh, A = πr², V = πr²h, c² = a² + b², C = 2πr, V = (4/3)πr³, V = (1/3)πr²h, V = (1/3)lwh, both special right triangles (30-60-90 with sides x, x√3, 2x and 45-45-90 with sides s, s, s√2), plus the statements: 'The number of degrees of arc in a circle is 360. The number of radians of arc in a circle is 2π. The sum of the measures in degrees of the angles of a triangle is 180.' NOT on the sheet and therefore worth memorizing: the quadratic formula, the discriminant, slope formula, arc length and sector area, the equation of a circle, SOHCAHTOA, and the exponential growth/decay form.

claims.claim: Khan Academy's Official SAT course mirrors the College Board taxonomy but adds a three-tier difficulty split
claims.detail: Khan Academy's v2 SAT Math course organizes content as the four College Board domains × three difficulty tiers — unit slugs are literally 'algebra-easier / algebra-medium / algebra-harder' (surfaced as Foundations / Medium / Advanced), with lesson names matching College Board testing points (e.g. 'Solving systems of linear equations: advanced', 'Systems of linear equations word problems', 'Graphs of linear equations and functions: advanced', 'Evaluating statistical claims'). For a 600–750 student the actionable use is to skip Foundations and Medium entirely and work only the '-harder' units of Advanced Math and Algebra. Note: the site is JavaScript-rendered and blocked my direct scrape, so the unit list here is assembled from indexed lesson URLs rather than a single fetched contents page.

claims.claim: PrepScholar's domain breakdown matches the official 13–15 / 13–15 / 5–7 / 5–7 counts
claims.detail: PrepScholar's topic article reports Algebra 13–15, Advanced Math 13–15, Problem Solving and Data Analysis 5–7, Geometry and Trigonometry 5–7, and notes geometry/trig is now a larger share than on the paper SAT (up to ~15% vs ~8%). It advises that over half the section is algebra and that this is where study time should concentrate. Useful as independent corroboration of the official table. Caveat: the College Board k12 alignment web page renders slightly different-looking counts in some summaries (15–16 / 7) — those appear to be percentages scaled against 44 rather than the 40 operational questions; the PDF tables (13–15 / 5–7) are authoritative.

claims.claim: Princeton Review: ~70% of the Math section is algebra 'in one form or another'; ~11 SPR questions
claims.detail: Princeton Review's digital SAT guides state the four domains at ~35/35/15/15, note that approximately 11 of the 44 Math questions require entering an answer in five characters or fewer, confirm 22 questions per module with 20 scored and 2 experimental, and state that questions within each module run in order of difficulty with the hardest toward the end. Their framing that Algebra + Advanced Math ≈ 70% of the test is a useful planning heuristic and is consistent with the official ≈35% + ≈35%.

claims.claim: What makes questions hard (reputational): multi-concept, multi-step, many variables, convoluted wording
claims.detail: PrepScholar's analysis of the hardest SAT math questions identifies five difficulty drivers: multiple concepts tested at once, long multi-step solutions ('the more steps you need to take, the easier to mess up somewhere'), less-practiced concepts (functions), convoluted phrasing that obscures what is asked, and problems with many variables. Named topic areas for the hardest questions: advanced algebra (systems and polynomial expressions), functions, coordinate geometry, and trigonometry. Named high-scorer failure modes: misreading and solving for the wrong variable, and setup errors translating a word problem into an equation. Caveat: this article predates/straddles the digital transition and mentions complex numbers, which are NOT in the digital SAT testing-point taxonomy — treat that item as stale.

claims.claim: Erica Meltzer / The Critical Reader has no digital-SAT MATH difficulty analysis to cite
claims.detail: The Critical Reader's catalog and digital-SAT article archive are Reading and Writing only — Meltzer's books and her question-by-category indexes cover R&W, not Math. I found no Math difficulty taxonomy from this source. Reporting this as a negative result rather than substituting a lower-quality source. Kaplan's digital SAT guide returned HTTP 403 and could not be verified either, so any Kaplan-attributed claim in this report would be unsourced.

claims.claim: ~30% of Math questions are set in context, and most in-context questions are short
claims.detail: Framework §4.1.7 and §4.1.8: approximately 30 percent of Math questions (10–14 of the 40 operational) are set in a science, social studies, or real-world context, and a majority of in-context questions are 50 standardized (six-character) words or fewer. Topic-specific prior knowledge is never assessed. Practical read: the digital SAT deliberately stripped heavy reading load out of Math, so a 600–750 student's errors are much more likely to be setup/algebra errors than comprehension errors.

night_before_priorities: SPR entry rules and the official examples table (~5 minutes, protects ~8-12 questions). Memorize: mixed numbers must be improper fractions or decimals (3 1/2 is REJECTED, 7/2 and 3.5 accepted); 5 characters positive / 6 negative counting the decimal point and fraction bar; for repeating decimals FILL the field (0.666 or 0.667 accepted, 0.66 and 0.67 REJECTED); no %, $, or comma; unreduced fractions and trailing zeros are fine. This is pure mechanics with zero conceptual load and the single highest points-per-minute item on the test.

Number-of-solutions conditions (~10 minutes, hits both 13-15 question domains). Discriminant b^2-4ac > 0 / = 0 / < 0 for quadratics; for two linear equations, same slope + different intercept = no solution, same slope + same intercept = infinitely many, different slopes = exactly one. College Board names this explicitly as a band 6 (610-670) discriminator in BOTH Algebra and Advanced Math, and it appears as 'find a possible second equation' and 'find the value of the unknown constant' variants.

Desmos workflow drill for Algebra + Advanced Math (~20 minutes, covers ~70% of the section). Graph both sides and read intersections instead of solving nonlinear systems by hand; type the equation with a letter constant to auto-create a slider and solve 'find the value of a' problems visually; use a table + regression for two-variable data; read vertex/intercepts/zeros straight off the graph. This converts the two heaviest domains from algebra fluency (unimprovable overnight) into a mechanical skill (improvable overnight).

Circles formulas (~10 minutes, SAT-only, band 7, NOT on the reference sheet). Equation (x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2 and completing the square to get there; arc length = (theta/360)*2*pi*r; sector area = (theta/360)*pi*r^2; radians = degrees * pi/180; tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact; central angle = 2x inscribed angle on the same arc. Guaranteed presence in the 5-7 Geo/Trig block, explicitly named in the band 7 statement, and the reference sheet gives you nothing here.

Trig facts (~8 minutes, band 7). sin(theta) = cos(90 - theta) and cos(theta) = sin(90 - theta) is named verbatim in the band 7 statement; SOHCAHTOA; degree-radian conversion. The 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles ARE printed on the reference sheet, so do not spend a second memorizing them - just know they are there.

Scale factor effects (~3 minutes, band 6). Multiply every length by k and perimeter scales by k, area by k^2, volume by k^3. One line, explicitly named in the official band 6 Geometry statement, and it converts an otherwise-hard similar-solids question into arithmetic.

Exponential form and function translations (~10 minutes, band 6/7). y = a(b)^x with b = 1 + r for growth and 1 - r for decay (an 80% decrease means b = 0.2, not 0.8 - this is the classic trap); and f(x - h) + k shifts right h and up k. 'How a translation of a function affects the key features of the graph or the equation' is named verbatim in the band 6 Advanced Math statement.

Percent and derived units (~8 minutes, band 6). Percent increase/decrease, reverse percent (find the original from the result), successive percent changes, and unit rates formed by products and quotients. The band 6 PSDA statement is literally 'solve multistep problems using ratios, rates, percentages, and derived units, including units that arise from products and quotients.' Small question count but very high fix rate per minute.

Statistics concepts, not computation (~10 minutes, band 6/7). How mean, median, and range shift when a value is added/removed/changed; why outliers pull the mean but not the median; how to compare two distributions' spread by eye; conditional probability from a two-way table (the whole skill is picking the correct denominator row or column). Never calculate a standard deviation - the SAT only asks you to compare.

Inference vocabulary (~5 minutes, band 7, but likely only ~1 question). Random SAMPLING lets you generalize to the population; random ASSIGNMENT lets you claim causation; a larger sample narrows the margin of error; a confidence interval is a plausible range for the population parameter, not for individuals. Band 7 names 'identify or describe the population to which the results of a research study can reasonably be extended.' Cheap because it is pure vocabulary, ranked low only because the expected question count is under 1.

Do NOT try to build Equivalent-expressions fluency overnight. Rewriting rational and radical expressions 'using structure' is a band 7 Advanced Math skill and is high-frequency, but it is a fluency, not a fact - a night of study moves it very little. Instead, note that on test day most of these can be brute-forced by plugging a number (say x = 3) into the original and each answer choice in Desmos and matching outputs. That tactic is learnable in 5 minutes; the underlying algebra is not.

Do NOT restudy linear equations and systems. This is the single highest-frequency block on the test, but a student already scoring 600-750 has it. Time spent here has near-zero marginal return. The one exception is the number-of-solutions variant in priority 2, which is a genuinely distinct band 6 skill.

Test-day structure facts worth 60 seconds of reading. 44 questions, two 35-minute modules of 22, ~1.59 min/question. Questions run easiest-to-hardest WITHIN each module, so never let a hard question at the end of module 1 eat the time budget. Module 1 performance decides which module 2 you receive and you cannot go back, so early accuracy sets the ceiling. Two questions per module are unscored pretest items placed anywhere in the sequence - a bizarre-looking question may simply not count.

result.summary:
The Digital SAT Reading and Writing section is fully specified in public College Board documents, and two of them answer the structural questions definitively: the *Digital SAT Suite of Assessments Specifications Overview* and the far longer *Assessment Framework for the Digital SAT Suite*. Both state the four content domains with official weights (Craft and Structure ≈28% / 13–15 questions; Information and Ideas ≈26% / 12–14; Standard English Conventions ≈26% / 11–15; Expression of Ideas ≈20% / 8–12) and both state the module architecture: 54 questions total, two 32-minute modules of 27 questions each (25 operational + 2 embedded pretest), 64 minutes, averaging 1.19 minutes per question, every question discrete with its own 25–150-word passage and four choices. Critically, Table 9 of the Assessment Framework ("Reading and Writing Section Question Sequence") publishes the domain order explicitly and identically for both modules: Craft and Structure → Information and Ideas → Standard English Conventions → Expression of Ideas. The framework further states the ordering rule inside each block: "Within each content domain except Standard English Conventions, questions are ordered first by skill/knowledge element and then by question difficulty from easiest to hardest," while "Standard English Conventions questions are ordered from easiest to hardest irrespective of skill/knowledge element tested." That last clause matters strategically — the grammar block is the one place where you cannot predict which rule is coming, only that difficulty is climbing.

What is *not* official is the order of individual question types inside each domain block; College Board publishes the skill/knowledge testing points but not their sequence. Reputable prep sources that have mapped released official practice tests converge on: Words in Context → Text Structure and Purpose → Cross-Text Connections → Central Ideas and Details → Command of Evidence (Textual, then Quantitative) → Inferences → [Standard English Conventions, difficulty-sorted, rules interleaved] → Transitions → Rhetorical Synthesis. I have marked that as reputable rather than official, and flagged the one sub-ordering (Command of Evidence vs. Inferences) that I could not corroborate across independent sources. Likewise, the granular list of 15-ish grammar rules is a prep-community synthesis, not a College Board enumeration — College Board names only two testing points (Boundaries; Form, Structure, and Sense) and describes their scope in prose, which I quote. All research came from published specification documents, official policy pages, and mainstream prep publishers; no recalled-item sources of any kind were consulted, opened, or used.

claims.claim: The four R&W content domains and their official weights and question counts
claims.detail:
From the College Board Specifications Overview, Table 2 (identical figures repeat in the Assessment Framework, Tables 11–14):

• Craft and Structure — approximately 28% of operational questions / 13–15 questions. Testing points: Words in Context; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections.
• Information and Ideas — approximately 26% / 12–14 questions. Testing points: Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence (Textual and Quantitative); Inferences.
• Standard English Conventions — approximately 26% / 11–15 questions. Testing points: Boundaries; Form, Structure, and Sense.
• Expression of Ideas — approximately 20% / 8–12 questions. Testing points: Rhetorical Synthesis; Transitions.

Note the counts are of OPERATIONAL questions (50 of the 54; 4 are unscored pretest items indistinguishable from the rest), so the percentages are of 50, not 54.

Official domain definitions, verbatim from the Specifications Overview:
- Craft and Structure: 'Measures the comprehension, vocabulary, analysis, synthesis, and reasoning skills and knowledge needed to understand and use high-utility words and phrases in context, evaluate texts rhetorically, and make connections between topically related texts.'
- Information and Ideas: 'Measures comprehension, analysis, and reasoning skills and knowledge and the ability to locate, interpret, evaluate, and integrate information and ideas from texts and informational graphics (tables, bar graphs, and line graphs).'
- Standard English Conventions: 'Measures the ability to edit texts to conform to core conventions of Standard English sentence structure, usage, and punctuation.'
- Expression of Ideas: 'Measures the ability to revise texts to improve the effectiveness of written expression and to meet specific rhetorical goals.'

Strategic read: Craft and Structure is the largest domain, but it is also the one most dependent on reading ability, which is slow to move. Standard English Conventions is nearly the same size (11–15 questions) and rests on a closed, memorizable rule set. That asymmetry is the whole basis of the night-before ranking below.
