claims.claim: Official section architecture: 54 questions, two 32-minute modules, adaptive routing, 1.19 min/question
claims.detail:
From the Assessment Framework, section 3.1 and Table 8:

• Administration: two-stage adaptive design. Module 1 (the 'routing' module) is a broad mix of easy, medium, and hard questions. Module 2's average difficulty is targeted to your Module 1 performance — you receive an on-average-harder or on-average-easier second module.
• Test length: Module 1 = 25 operational + 2 pretest; Module 2 = 25 operational + 2 pretest. Total 54 questions.
• Time: 32 minutes per module, 64 minutes total. Average 1.19 minutes per question.
• Question format: 'Discrete; four-option multiple-choice.' Every question has its own passage — there are no shared-passage question sets on the digital SAT at all.
• Word count: '25–150 (6-character) words per stimulus text (or pair of texts).'
• Passage subject areas: literature, history/social studies, the humanities, science. Informational graphics are limited to tables, bar graphs, and line graphs.
• Text complexity bands: grades 6–8, 9–11, 12–14.
• Scoring: section score 200–800, half the total score. Pretest questions do not count.
• Navigation: 'Students may navigate freely through a given module' — you can preview ahead and flag questions to return to. But once Bluebook advances you to Module 2 you cannot return to Module 1, and once it advances you to Math you cannot return to R&W at all.

Official statement worth internalizing: 'all the information needed to answer each question is provided in the passage or passages themselves' — no outside topic knowledge is ever required.

claims.claim: THE DOMAIN ORDER IS OFFICIALLY PUBLISHED — Assessment Framework Table 9
claims.detail:
This is the precise, citable answer to the ordering question. The Assessment Framework contains 'Table 9. Reading and Writing Section Question Sequence,' which lists, identically for Module 1 and Module 2:

  1. Craft and Structure questions
  2. Information and Ideas questions
  3. Standard English Conventions questions
  4. Expression of Ideas questions

The Specifications Overview states the same thing in prose: 'Questions from all four domains appear in each Reading and Writing test module, beginning with Craft and Structure questions and then continuing through Information and Ideas, Standard English Conventions, and Expression of Ideas questions.'

The within-block ordering rule, verbatim from the Assessment Framework: 'Within each content domain except Standard English Conventions, questions are ordered first by skill/knowledge element and then by question difficulty from easiest to hardest. Standard English Conventions questions are ordered from easiest to hardest irrespective of skill/knowledge element tested.'

And the rationale, from the Specifications Overview: questions testing similar skills 'are grouped together to reduce the need for context switching and arranged from easiest to hardest. This makes it easier for students to budget their time.'

One more official detail with practical value: 'Embedded pretest questions appear alongside questions testing the same skill/knowledge element (or, in the case of Standard English Conventions pretest questions, among the operational questions in that content domain).' So pretest items do not disturb the sequence — you cannot spot them, and you should not try.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES:
(a) Difficulty is a sawtooth, not a ramp. It resets at the start of every skill group. A question that follows a brutal one may be easy — never let a hard question poison your read of the next one.
(b) You always know roughly where you are. Questions with two passages labeled 'Text 1 / Text 2' mark the end of Craft and Structure. The first 'Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?' marks the start of the grammar block. The first bulleted-notes question means you are in the final stretch.
(c) The grammar block is the one place you cannot anticipate the rule, only the rising difficulty. Do not expect all the commas together.
(d) The last few questions of the module are the hardest Rhetorical Synthesis items. If you are burning time early, you are spending it on questions that are, by design, easier than the ones you will never reach.

claims.claim: Question-type order INSIDE each domain block (reputable mapping, not officially published)
claims.detail:
College Board publishes that questions are ordered 'first by skill/knowledge element' but does not publish which element comes first. Prep publishers that have mapped the released official practice tests report this consistent sequence:

  1. Words in Context            ┐
  2. Text Structure and Purpose  ├ Craft and Structure
  3. Cross-Text Connections      ┘
  4. Central Ideas and Details   ┐
  5. Command of Evidence: Textual├ Information and Ideas
  6. Command of Evidence: Quantitative
  7. Inferences                  ┘
  8. Standard English Conventions — Boundaries and Form/Structure/Sense INTERLEAVED, sorted purely by difficulty (this part IS official)
  9. Transitions                 ┐ Expression of Ideas
 10. Rhetorical Synthesis        ┘

Test Innovators states it directly: 'The testing points always appear in the same order, and the questions within each testing point are presented in order of increasing difficulty' — so a module opens with the easiest Words in Context question and closes with the hardest Rhetorical Synthesis question.

CAVEAT I could not fully resolve: the relative position of Command of Evidence vs. Inferences within Information and Ideas is corroborated by only one source family. Treat items 4–7 as 'these four types, in roughly this order' rather than as a guarantee. The domain-level order (claim above) is the part that is officially documented and safe to rely on.

Approximate per-type counts per full 54-question test, from PrepScholar's analysis of official practice tests — REPUTABLE ESTIMATE, NOT OFFICIAL, and these will vary form to form:
• Words in Context ~10–11 (the single largest type, roughly a fifth of the section)
• Transitions ~5–6
• Rhetorical Synthesis ~5–6
• Boundaries ~5–6
• Form, Structure, and Sense ~7–8
• Central Ideas and Details ~4–5
• Command of Evidence Textual ~4
• Command of Evidence Quantitative ~3–4
• Inferences ~3–4
• Text Structure and Purpose ~2
• Cross-Text Connections ~1–2

claims.claim: Standard English Conventions — official scope statement from College Board
claims.detail:
College Board names only two testing points and describes their scope in prose. This is the authoritative boundary of what can be tested — quoted from the Assessment Framework:

BOUNDARIES — 'students must edit text to ensure that sentences are conventionally complete.' Expanded in Chapter 5: 'Boundaries questions require test takers to apply Standard English conventions when editing short texts (typically one or two sentences in length) to ensure that the resultant sentence(s) conventionally separate or join phrases, clauses, or sentences. These questions address such matters as standard end punctuation, semicolon and colon use, and the conventional use (or nonuse) of punctuation, such as commas, dashes, and parentheses, to set off (or not set off) information and ideas within sentences.'

FORM, STRUCTURE, AND SENSE — 'students must edit text to conform to conventional usage (e.g., agreement, verb tense/aspect).' Expanded: these questions 'assess test takers' ability to apply core Standard English grammar and usage conventions in context, such as ensuring subject-verb agreement, using verb tenses and aspects appropriately, and appropriately forming and using plurals and genitives (possessives).'

Note the phrase 'the conventional use (OR NONUSE) of punctuation.' The framework's own published sample Boundaries question has the correct answer 'no punctuation at all,' with all three distractors inserting an unnecessary comma, colon, or semicolon between a long subject and its verb. That is College Board telling you, in its own document, that 'no punctuation' is a live and frequently correct answer.

The published sample Form/Structure/Sense question is a dangling modifier item — the three wrong answers 'all result in dangling modifiers.' Again, College Board signposting its favorite trap.

claims.claim: The finite Standard English Conventions rule list, with the single most common trap for each
claims.detail:
College Board does not enumerate rules; this list is the prep-community synthesis (PrepScholar, Test Innovators) mapped onto College Board's two official testing points. It is finite and it is closed — this is the whole grammar universe of the test.

=== BOUNDARIES (punctuation / sentence structure) ===

1. SENTENCE BOUNDARIES — fragments, run-ons, comma splices.
   Rule: two independent clauses need period, semicolon, colon, dash, or comma+FANBOYS.
   #1 TRAP: the comma splice disguised by a conjunctive adverb. 'however,' 'therefore,' 'moreover,' 'consequently,' 'in addition' are NOT coordinating conjunctions — a comma before them still leaves a splice. Students see a logical connector and accept the comma. Only the semicolon version is correct.

2. SEMICOLONS.
   Rule: independent clause on BOTH sides (sole exception: 'super-comma' in a list whose items already contain commas).
   #1 TRAP: the material after the semicolon is a fragment — a participial phrase or a 'which/because' clause — and it reads smoothly, so it passes the ear test. Test both halves independently.

3. COLONS.
   Rule: what comes BEFORE must be a complete sentence; what comes after need not be.
   #1 TRAP: a colon after an incomplete lead-in, especially after 'such as,' 'including,' 'are,' or a preposition ('the study focused on:'). Also colon-vs-semicolon confusion when the second half is a list or explanation.

4. DASHES.
   Rule: a pair of dashes brackets a non-essential element; a single dash works like a colon or a strong comma.
   #1 TRAP: mismatched pair — a dash opening the interruption and a comma closing it (or vice versa). Both marks must match. Scan for the opening mark before judging the closing one.

5. COMMAS AND NON-ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS.
   Rule: non-essential info takes paired commas mid-sentence, one comma at the start or end.
   #1 TRAP: the unpaired comma — one comma dropped into the middle of an interrupting phrase. Also the classic: NO comma between a subject and its verb, no matter how long the subject grows. College Board's own sample question is exactly this.

6. ESSENTIAL vs. NON-ESSENTIAL (restrictive vs. non-restrictive).
   Rule: if removing it changes which thing you mean, it is essential and takes no commas.
   #1 TRAP: commas around a name or title that is essential to identifying the noun ('the biologist, Jane Doe, discovered' vs. 'the biologist Jane Doe discovered'). Ask: does the sentence still identify the right person without it?

7. NO-PUNCTUATION ITEMS.
   #1 TRAP: assuming a punctuation question must want punctuation. When all four choices differ only by mark, 'no punctuation' is a real contender — check whether you would be severing subject from verb, verb from object, or a preposition from its object.

=== FORM, STRUCTURE, AND SENSE (grammar / usage) ===

8. SUBJECT-VERB AGREEMENT.
   #1 TRAP: deliberate distance between subject and verb — an intervening prepositional phrase, non-essential appositive, or relative clause whose noun has the opposite number. Cross out everything between commas and read subject straight into verb. Secondary traps: inverted order ('There are/is...'), singular-looking-plural subjects (each, every, either, neither, the number of), and collective nouns treated as singular.

9. PRONOUN-ANTECEDENT AGREEMENT.
   #1 TRAP: a singular antecedent ('a researcher,' 'the company,' 'each participant') paired with 'they/their.' Natural in speech, wrong on the test. Also 'it/its' for institutions and collective nouns.

10. PRONOUN AMBIGUITY / CLARITY.
   #1 TRAP: a pronoun with two grammatically possible antecedents; the correct answer usually repeats the noun instead of using the pronoun. (Frequency note: this is a well-documented prep category but is not named in College Board's official scope prose — treat it as lower-frequency than 8 and 9.)

11. VERB TENSE AND ASPECT.
   #1 TRAP: the answer is decided entirely by a time cue elsewhere in the passage — a date, 'currently,' 'in the 1890s,' 'since' — not by anything inside the underlined portion. Students pick by ear. Find the time marker first. Use past perfect only when two past events genuinely need sequencing.

12. VERB FORM — finite vs. non-finite.
   #1 TRAP: a choice offering an -ing form, a participle, or 'having been' where the clause needs a real conjugated main verb — producing a fragment. This is where Boundaries and Form/Structure/Sense overlap, and it catches strong students because the phrasing sounds sophisticated.

13. MODIFIER PLACEMENT (dangling / misplaced).
   #1 TRAP: an introductory participial or 'Based on…' phrase followed by the wrong noun. The word immediately after the comma must be the thing the phrase describes. This is College Board's published sample trap, and prep sources report it appears on essentially every form. Note this often disguises itself as a 'which choice completes the text' question with four full clause rewrites.

14. PARALLELISM.
   #1 TRAP: a choice that is perfectly grammatical in isolation but does not match the form of the other list items — gerund among infinitives, noun among verbs. Also correlative pairs: 'not only X but also Y' and 'both X and Y' require matching forms on each side.

15. POSSESSIVES vs. PLURALS.
   #1 TRAP: all four choices are the same word in four forms (dog / dogs / dog's / dogs') and only the sentence's logic distinguishes them. Ask two questions in order: how many? and does something belong to it? Also the homophone set: its/it's, their/there/they're, whose/who's, your/you're.

16. NOUN NUMBER LOGIC.
   #1 TRAP: singular noun where the logic demands plural — 'the students raised their hand.' Multiple owners, multiple objects.

Bonus, carried over from the pre-digital SAT and still reported by prep sources but NOT confirmed in College Board's current scope prose — treat as lower priority: illogical comparisons ('unlike Shakespeare, Marlowe's plays…'; 'better than any other,' not 'better than any'), who vs. whom, and subject vs. object pronoun case.

claims.claim: Transitions: the standard method and the wrong-answer patterns
claims.detail:
OFFICIAL DEFINITION: 'Transitions, for which students must determine the most effective transition word or phrase to logically connect information and ideas in a text.' (Assessment Framework, Table 13.) ~5–6 questions per test, appearing immediately after the grammar block.

THE METHOD every reputable source teaches — the order of operations is the whole technique:
1. COVER THE ANSWER CHOICES. Do not read them yet. This is not a tip; it is the method.
2. Read the sentence before the blank and the sentence after, in full.
3. Paraphrase each in one short clause, stripping the academic vocabulary.
4. NAME the relationship out loud in one word before looking down: continue / contrast / cause-effect / example / sequence / emphasis. Many teachers compress this to three buckets — Continuers, Contradictors, Cause-and-Effect — because that trichotomy alone eliminates two to three choices instantly.
5. Only now read the choices, and keep only those in your named category.
6. If two survive, re-read for direction: which sentence causes which.

WRONG-ANSWER PATTERNS:
• The right word for the WRONG relationship. This is the dominant pattern: 'therefore' offered on a contrast item, 'however' on a pure continuation, 'for example' when the second sentence is a consequence rather than an illustration. Each distractor is a perfectly good transition — for a sentence you are not reading.
• Momentum bias. The student stays locked in sentence 1's framing because sentence 2 is still about the same experiment or the same researcher, and picks 'therefore' or 'so' when the content has quietly reversed. Same topic ≠ same direction.
• Addition mistaken for emphasis. 'Furthermore / in addition' vs. 'indeed / in fact' both feel like agreement; only one is intensifying the same claim rather than adding a new one.
• Sounding right. Working backward from the choices makes you pick on rhythm and register instead of logic. This is precisely what step 1 prevents.

A free elimination heuristic: if two choices mean substantially the same thing (e.g., 'however' and 'nevertheless'), neither can be correct — the SAT will not offer two right answers. Cross both out and choose among the rest.

claims.claim: Rhetorical Synthesis: the standard method and the wrong-answer patterns
claims.detail:
OFFICIAL DEFINITION: 'Rhetorical Synthesis, for which students must strategically integrate provided information and ideas on a topic to form an effective sentence achieving a specified rhetorical aim.' (Assessment Framework, Table 13.) ~5–6 per test, and they are ALWAYS the last questions of each module — the officially hardest items you will face.

STRUCTURE: a one-line setup, a bulleted list of notes, then a stated goal ('The student wants to…') and the stem 'Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?'

THE METHOD:
1. SKIP THE BULLETS ENTIRELY on first pass. Go straight to the goal sentence. Reading the notes first is the single biggest time sink in the section.
2. Restate the goal in six words or fewer, with attention to the VERB: emphasize, compare, contrast, explain, introduce, summarize, illustrate with a concrete example, present the finding to an audience unfamiliar with the topic.
3. Note whether the goal is two-part ('make a generalization AND support it with a specific detail'). If so, both halves are required.
4. Go to the choices and test each against the goal alone. Ask 'does this sentence perform that rhetorical action?' — not 'is this true?'
5. Use the bullets only to confirm a finalist or break a tie.

THE CENTRAL INSIGHT that separates a 700 from a 750 here: every choice is factually accurate and drawn from the notes. Truth is not the discriminator. Only goal-fulfillment is. If you find yourself checking whether a statement is supported by the bullets, you are answering the wrong question.

WRONG-ANSWER PATTERNS:
• TRUE BUT OFF-GOAL — the dominant trap. Accurately combines notes, reads beautifully, does not do what the goal asked.
• PARTIAL FULFILLMENT — satisfies one half of a two-part goal. Makes the generalization but never supports it; compares but never explains. The 'good enough' answer instead of the 'just right' one.
• RIGHT NOTES, WRONG EMPHASIS — uses the correct material but frames it backwards, e.g. presenting a similarity as a contrast, or foregrounding the detail that the goal wanted subordinated.
• WRONG RHETORICAL MOVE — explains when the goal asked to compare; describes when it asked to introduce.
• INVENTS INFORMATION — slips in a causal claim where the notes showed only correlation, or adds an evaluative adjective the notes do not support.
• AUDIENCE MISMATCH — the goal specifies a reader unfamiliar with the topic, and the choice assumes background knowledge (or vice versa: over-explains for a specialist audience).

claims.claim: Words in Context: the method and the traps
claims.detail:
OFFICIAL DEFINITION: 'Words in Context, for which students must determine the meaning of a high-utility academic word or phrase in context or use such vocabulary in a precise, contextually appropriate way.' (Assessment Framework, Table 11.) The largest single question type — roughly a fifth of the section — and the FIRST questions of every module, meaning they are also, by the ordering rule, among the easiest questions you will see. The last two or three in the block are where 600–750 students actually lose points.

TWO FORMATS:
(a) Fill-in-the-blank: 'Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?'
(b) Underlined word: 'As used in the text, what does the word X most nearly mean?'

THE METHOD:
1. Read the whole short passage, plus the sentence before and after the blank — these passages are 25–150 words, so 'whole passage' is cheap.
2. COVER THE CHOICES and predict your own word. Even a clumsy prediction ('something like *hidden*') is enough; the point is committing to a meaning before the distractors can bias you.
3. Determine the CHARGE first: positive, negative, or neutral. Charge alone kills one or two choices on most hard items.
4. Match your prediction to the closest choice.
5. Substitute the winner back into the original sentence and re-read the full sentence. If it distorts tone or forces you to reinterpret the rest of the sentence, it is wrong.

CRITICAL SIGNAL for the harder items: find the structural cue in the passage — a contrast marker ('but,' 'although,' 'despite'), a colon or dash introducing a definition, an appositive, or a parallel restatement. These questions are almost always solvable from a single syntactic relationship rather than from vocabulary knowledge.

TRAPS:
• THE COMMON-DEFINITION TRAP — the most familiar meaning of a familiar word. The test deliberately favors secondary and tertiary senses ('table,' 'novel,' 'qualify,' 'reserved,' 'arrest,' 'economy'). If a choice is the dictionary's first entry and it fits comfortably, be suspicious.
• DICTIONARY-VALID DISTRACTORS — every choice is a genuine definition of the word or a genuine English word; only one fits THIS context. Vocabulary recognition alone will not separate them.
• CONNOTATION / CHARGE MISMATCH — a choice with the right denotation but the wrong emotional register. 'Persuade' where the passage's disapproving tone demands 'cajole.'
• TOO STRONG / TOO WEAK — a near-match that overshoots ('devastated' for 'disappointed') or undershoots. Very common in the last items of the block.
• OUT OF SCOPE — introduces a concept the passage never raises.
• READING THE CHOICES FIRST — the root cause of most of the above.

On cramming vocabulary: UWorld and other reputable publishers state explicitly that you 'do not need to memorize long vocabulary lists' because the test prioritizes contextual reasoning. College Board's framework confirms it selects 'high-utility academic words' that appear across disciplines. The night before, a word list is a poor use of time; the predict-and-substitute discipline is not.

claims.claim: Cross-Text Connections (the paired/dual passages): the method and the traps
claims.detail:
OFFICIAL DEFINITION: 'Cross-Text Connections, for which students must draw a reasonable connection between two topically related texts.' (Assessment Framework, Table 11.) These are the only questions on the digital SAT presenting two passages, labeled Text 1 and Text 2, sharing the same 25–150-word budget between them. They sit at the END of the Craft and Structure block, so they are the hardest questions in that domain — and their position is a reliable landmark that Information and Ideas is about to start.

COUNT: UNVERIFIED / sources conflict. PrepScholar's practice-test analysis puts it near 1–2 per full test; another prep source claims 2–3 per module. Given Craft and Structure is 13–15 questions covering three testing points and Words in Context alone takes ~10, the low estimate is far more plausible. Plan for one or two, not six.

THE METHOD:
1. Read Text 1 for exactly one thing: the author's CLAIM, in one plain sentence. Strip the evidence, keep the position.
2. Do the same for Text 2. Write or subvocalize both one-liners.
3. NAME the relationship before reading the choices — same discipline as Transitions:
   • AGREE — same conclusion, possibly via different evidence
   • DISAGREE — opposite conclusions, or one challenges the other's evidence or reasoning
   • EXTEND — Text 2 builds a new, consistent angle without contradicting
   • QUALIFY — Text 2 accepts part of Text 1 but adds a condition, exception, or limitation
4. Identify WHO the question is asking about. The stem almost always makes one author the actor: 'how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to…' Answer as that author, about the specific claim named — not about the topic in general.
5. Eliminate any choice that misstates either text on its own terms. A choice must be accurate about BOTH passages before its relationship can be right.

TRAPS:
• OVERSTATED OPPOSITION — the single most common. Students default to 'they completely disagree.' The test's favorite real relationship is partial agreement with one key difference (QUALIFY), and the distractors reward the blunt reading.
• RIGHT RELATIONSHIP, WRONG CLAIM — correctly identifies disagreement, but about a point Text 2 never addressed.
• ACCURATE ABOUT ONE TEXT ONLY — flawless summary of Text 1, invented content for Text 2. Verify both halves separately.
• AGREEMENT SMUGGLED IN — a choice asserting the authors agree on something neither actually claimed.
• Note: when a stem asks how one author would 'respond to' or 'say about' the other, the answer is nearly always some form of disagreement or qualification — pure agreement makes for a weak question, so the test rarely writes one.

night_before_priorities: 1. THE BOUNDARIES DECISION TREE (highest points per minute, by a wide margin). Roughly 5-6 questions per test, and they collapse to one mechanical procedure: cover the answer choices, read the material before the blank and after the blank, and ask only 'is each side an independent clause?' Both independent -> period, semicolon, colon, dash, or comma+FANBOYS. One side dependent or a phrase -> comma or nothing. Then check whether you are severing a subject from its verb, in which case the answer is no punctuation at all. Fifteen minutes on this, and the three specific traps (conjunctive adverbs like 'however' are not conjunctions; a colon needs a complete sentence before it; dashes and commas must match as a pair), is the best-converting study of the night for someone already at 600-750.

2. THE GRAMMAR RULE AUDIT, but only your misses. Standard English Conventions is 11-15 questions of a closed rule set - the only domain where the material is genuinely finite and memorizable. Do not re-read all sixteen rules. Take the list, and for each one ask 'could I state the rule and its trap right now?' Study only the ones where the answer is no. For most students in this band the gaps cluster in three places: subject-verb agreement across a long interrupter, dangling modifiers after an introductory phrase (College Board's own published sample trap, reported on essentially every form), and the four-way possessive/plural choice. Twenty minutes.

3. THE TWO 'COVER THE CHOICES' DRILLS - Transitions and Rhetorical Synthesis. About 11 questions combined, and both are won by the same act of discipline: naming the answer before you look. For Transitions, name the relationship (continue / contrast / cause-effect) out loud before reading a single choice; two or three distractors die instantly, and the dominant trap - the right word for the wrong relationship - stops working. For Rhetorical Synthesis, read the goal FIRST and skip the bullets entirely, then reject every choice that does not perform the stated rhetorical action no matter how true it is. Internalize the one sentence that governs the whole type: every choice is factually accurate; truth is not the discriminator. Fifteen minutes total, and it also buys back time on the hardest questions in the section.

4. THE MAP OF THE MODULE (five minutes, disproportionate payoff). Memorize the official order - Craft and Structure, then Information and Ideas, then Standard English Conventions, then Expression of Ideas - and the fact that difficulty resets to easy at the start of every skill group rather than climbing monotonically. Three consequences to hold onto: a brutal question is often followed by an easy one, so never let one poison the next; the appearance of 'Text 1 / Text 2' means Craft and Structure is ending; and the bulleted-notes questions at the very end are the hardest items on the module, so time spent stuck early is being taken from questions that are easier than the ones you will never reach. Also remember you can navigate and flag freely within a module but can never return once it closes.

5. WORDS IN CONTEXT: charge before meaning. It is the largest single type (~10-11 questions) but it opens the module, so a 600-750 student is already banking most of them - the marginal points are in the last two or three of the block. Do not open a vocabulary list; reputable publishers and College Board's own construct description both point away from memorization. Instead rehearse two habits: decide positive / negative / neutral before you read the choices, and be suspicious of any answer that is the word's most familiar meaning. Ten minutes.

6. CROSS-TEXT CONNECTIONS: one sentence per text, then name the relationship. Only about one or two questions per test, so it ranks below everything above on volume - but the method is nearly free to learn and the trap is a single predictable one. Reduce each text to its claim in one plain sentence, then choose among agree / disagree / extend / qualify, and resist the pull toward total opposition; partial agreement with one key difference is the test's favorite real answer. Five minutes.

7. WHAT NOT TO DO TONIGHT. Do not take a full practice test - the fatigue cost outweighs any diagnostic value the night before. Do not memorize vocabulary lists. Do not study Text Structure and Purpose (roughly 2 questions) or drill Command of Evidence Quantitative technique from scratch; both are low-volume or reading-dependent, and reading ability does not move overnight. If time remains after items 1-6, re-read your own recent wrong answers and label each with which trap caught you - that is worth more than any new material.

So module 1 + the module 2 a student actually receives is a FORM. A PANEL is three modules (routing module plus BOTH possible second-stage modules); the student sees only two of the panel's three. corrections.correction: Date list confirmed exactly as published: Aug 23 2026, Sept 20 2026, Oct 18 2026, Nov 8 2026, Dec 6 2026, Mar 7 2027, May 2 2027, June 6 2027. corrections.original_claim: The Sept and Oct Sundays are shifted because the adjacent Sundays fall on Jewish High Holy Days
corrections.correction: The DATES are official; the REASON is the brief's own inference and is not published by College Board. College Board states only the general rule ('unless that Sunday is a religious holiday') and never names which holiday moved which date. The inference is at least arithmetically consistent — Sept 13, 2026 and Oct 4, 2026 are both Sundays and both fall on Jewish holidays (Rosh Hashanah day 2 and Simchat Torah respectively, in Hebrew year 5787) — but it does not explain the full shift (Oct 11, 2026 is an ordinary Sunday yet the published date is Oct 18). Present the dates as official and the rationale as unsourced. Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/help-center/what-sunday-dates-are-available

corrections.original_claim: Sunday testing: religious-reason eligibility, signed letter on letterhead from a religious leader, Inquiry Form topic 'Registration' / detail 'Change Saturday/Sunday status', Saturday-or-Sunday-not-both, unavailable in India or Pakistan
corrections.correction: Every element confirmed on the official page, including the verbatim restriction 'For a particular test administration, you can take the test on Saturday or Sunday, but not both' and 'Sunday testing isn't available in India or Pakistan.' Documentation requirement confirmed: a letter from an official religious leader explaining the reason, bearing the leader's signature, on official stationery of the religious or educational organization. Process and admission-ticket step confirmed. Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/registration/additional-registration-options/sunday-testing

corrections.original_claim: Whether the Sunday form is the same test form as Saturday is NOT published by College Board — UNVERIFIED
corrections.correction: The UNVERIFIED marking is correct and appropriately handled. I independently checked the Sunday testing page, the Sunday-dates help-center article, the testing rules page, and the 2026-27 Student Guide: College Board publishes eligibility, documentation, dates, and the Saturday-or-Sunday restriction, and makes no statement about form identity. The brief's framing — that everything published (structure, timing, routing, scale, calculator/ID policy, score-release date) is identical for Sunday testers and that Sunday is a scheduling accommodation rather than a different product — is a fair characterization of the published record. Correctly refuses to assert either way. Sources: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/registration/additional-registration-options/sunday-testing ; https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/testing-rules

corrections.correction: All five fall 2026 pairs match the official score-release page exactly, and the quoted line is verbatim: 'Most scores from weekend tests are released 2–4 weeks after test day.' corrections.original_claim: Bluebook and device changes for 2026-27: Windows 11 required, ChromeOS 144 minimum, Chromebook verified mode, resizable calculator, alternate reference-sheet layout, zoom/pan on graphics, U.S. Waitlist, educator practice tests, Test Day Live
corrections.correction: Confirmed, with a sourcing note. The 2026-27 changes page confirms: 'Bluebook will require Windows 11, as Microsoft no longer supports Windows 10'; Chromebooks need verified mode; resizable embedded Math calculator; reference sheets with alternative layout options; zoom and pan for charts, graphs, and images; Waitlist for U.S. students when dates/centers are full; and Test Day Live ('Test coordinators can access the same information for all students in Test Day Live'). ChromeOS 144 is NOT on that page — it is on the Bluebook technical site ('Bluebook can't be installed on versions below ChromeOS 144'; ChromeOS Flex not supported), so cite bluebook.collegeboard.org for it. Educator sign-in with a professional account to take unscored full-length practice tests is confirmed on Bluebook's new-and-updated-features page. The brief omits one 2026-27 change worth adding: students approved for Text-to-Speech (Embedded) must now test at a center rather than remotely, and TTS/screen-reader users must bring their own wired non-Bluetooth headphones. Sources: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/testing-staff/changes ; https://bluebook.collegeboard.org/technology/devices/requirements/chromebook ; https://bluebook.collegeboard.org/test-admin/new-updated-features

corrections.original_claim: Calculator policy: embedded Desmos (graphing + scientific) for the whole Math section, approved bring-your-own non-CAS, calculator under the desk during Reading and Writing, CAS models named (TI-Nspire CAS, HP Prime, Casio ClassPad)
corrections.correction: Confirmed, including the named CAS models — the policy explicitly lists 'Casio: ClassPad 300, 330, or 400; ClassPad II (fx-CP400); ClassPad fx-CG 500 or fx-CG500; Algebra fx 2.0'; 'Hewlett Packard: HP Prime; HP 48GII'; 'Texas Instruments: TI-Nspire CAS, TI-Nspire CX II CAS.' Confirmed: Desmos embedded in Bluebook with graphing/scientific toggle, Math section only, and during Reading and Writing 'you must put the calculator under your desk at all times.' Also confirmed: no sharing calculators, battery-operated handheld only (no power cords). Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/what-to-bring-do/calculator-policy

corrections.original_claim: Students are asked to clear all saved formulas from a brought calculator before testing
corrections.correction: Imprecise paraphrase, and it understates the rule by calling it a request. The policy is mandatory and narrower in one respect, broader in another: 'You must remove programs that have algebra functionality (e.g., solving equations, expanding algebraic expressions, factoring algebraic expressions, etc.) from your calculator' AND 'You must remove any stored documents from your calculator.' It is not 'all saved formulas' — it is algebra-functionality programs plus stored documents, and both are requirements, not suggestions. Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/what-to-bring-do/calculator-policy

corrections.original_claim: ID requirements — digital IDs are NOT accepted; acceptable/unacceptable lists; 21+ need government photo ID; prior-year school ID valid through Dec 31
corrections.correction: Confirmed on the official page, including the explicit prohibition: 'Digital IDs or any electronic document presented on a device' are unacceptable, and 'The ID must be a physical ID.' Acceptable and unacceptable lists match as stated. Confirmed: 'Student ID cards aren't valid forms of identification for test takers who are 21 or older,' and a prior-year school ID remains valid 'through the end of December of the current calendar year.' Note the useful contrast the brief gets right: the ID must be physical, but the ADMISSION TICKET may be electronic — the Student Guide says 'Show your printed ticket or present it on your mobile device.' Sources: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/what-to-bring-do/id-requirements ; https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/sat-student-guide.pdf

corrections.original_claim: What to bring and what is banned on test day; Testing Rules page last revised May 19, 2026
corrections.correction: Confirmed, including the page's own date stamp 'Last Revised: May 19, 2026.' Bring list and ban list match. Two gaps worth filling: (a) the official ban list is longer than the brief's — it also names smart glasses, Apple Pencils and stylus pens, cameras and recording devices, watches with alarms or timers, hats or head coverings (except for medical or religious reasons), weapons or firearms, and 'any device with internet access or AI capability'; (b) the headphone exception the brief cites is real but comes from the 2026-27 changes page, not the rules page — students with text-to-speech or screen-reader accommodations 'are required to bring their own wired, non-Bluetooth headphones.' The sub-claim 'Close all applications other than Bluebook before the test begins' is standard Bluebook guidance but I could NOT locate it on the Testing Rules page or in the Student Guide — treat as UNVERIFIED at that source. Sources: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/testing-rules ; https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/testing-staff/changes

corrections.original_claim: Reading and Writing domain distribution: Information and Ideas ~26% (12-14), Craft and Structure ~28% (13-15), Expression of Ideas ~20% (8-12), Standard English Conventions ~26% (11-15), with the listed skills
corrections.correction: Every percentage, range, and skill list matches Framework Table 10 and the per-domain 'Proportion' lines exactly: Information and Ideas '≈26% / 12–14 questions' (Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence — Textual, Quantitative; Inferences); Craft and Structure '≈28% / 13–15 questions' (Words in Context; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections); Expression of Ideas '≈20% / 8–12 questions' (Rhetorical Synthesis; Transitions); Standard English Conventions '≈26% / 11–15 questions' (Boundaries; Form, Structure, and Sense). Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/assessment-framework-for-digital-sat-suite.pdf

corrections.original_claim: Within each Reading and Writing module, questions appear grouped by domain in the fixed sequence Information and Ideas, Craft and Structure, Expression of Ideas, Standard English Conventions
corrections.correction: WRONG ORDER — this is the Framework's chapter/table listing order, not the on-test sequence. Framework Table 9, 'Reading and Writing Section Question Sequence,' gives the actual order, identical for both modules: (1) Craft and Structure questions, (2) Information and Ideas questions, (3) Standard English Conventions questions, (4) Expression of Ideas questions. This matters for the pacing advice the brief builds on it: a student following the brief's order would expect grammar questions last when they actually come third, with Expression of Ideas (Rhetorical Synthesis and Transitions) closing each module. Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/assessment-framework-for-digital-sat-suite.pdf

corrections.original_claim: Within each domain except Standard English Conventions, questions are ordered easiest to hardest
corrections.correction: Misreads what the exception is about. Standard English Conventions IS ordered easiest to hardest — the Framework says so directly. The real distinction is the grouping layer: 'Within each content domain except Standard English Conventions, questions are ordered first by skill/knowledge element and then by question difficulty from easiest to hardest. Standard English Conventions questions are ordered from easiest to hardest irrespective of skill/knowledge element tested.' So all four domains ramp easiest→hardest; the other three additionally cluster by skill first, meaning difficulty resets at each SKILL boundary in those domains, not only at each domain boundary. That actually strengthens the brief's pacing point rather than weakening it, but the stated rule is wrong as written. Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/assessment-framework-for-digital-sat-suite.pdf

corrections.original_claim: Math domain distribution: Algebra 13-15, Advanced Math 13-15, Problem-Solving and Data Analysis 5-7, Geometry and Trigonometry 5-7, with the listed skills; Algebra + Advanced Math roughly 65-75% of Math
corrections.correction: Question counts and skill lists match Framework Table 16 exactly. The brief omits the published percentages, which are worth citing directly: Algebra '≈35% / 13–15 questions', Advanced Math '≈35% / 13–15 questions', Problem-Solving and Data Analysis '≈15% / 5–7 questions', Geometry and Trigonometry '≈15% / 5–7 questions'. So Algebra + Advanced Math is ≈70% by College Board's own figure (the brief's 65–75% is the correct count-derived range, 26–30 of 40 operational questions, but ≈70% is the published number and is cleaner to cite). Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/assessment-framework-for-digital-sat-suite.pdf

corrections.original_claim: The adaptive design should not change test-taking behavior; Framework says the design is fair and students are best served answering to the best of their ability
corrections.correction: The quotation is verbatim and in context. Framework §2.2.3 reports simulation studies of a high achiever deliberately missing routing-module questions to be sent to the easier module, and concludes: 'this student would likely earn a lower score than they would have had they answered each question to the best of their ability—in no small part because intentionally answering numerous first-module questions incorrectly would sharply limit their highest possible section score.' Then: 'Taken together, these results establish that the adaptive aspect of the digital SAT Suite tests is fair to all students and that students are best served by answering each digital SAT Suite test question to the best of their ability.' The 'sharply limit their highest possible section score' mechanism is the strongest anti-gaming fact available and the brief should quote it. Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/assessment-framework-for-digital-sat-suite.pdf

corrections.original_claim: There is no wrong-answer penalty, so leaving anything blank is never correct
corrections.correction: Directionally right, materially incomplete. There is no per-question guessing penalty — the Framework's 'Guessing on Digital SAT Suite Questions' sidebar says the IRT model's evaluation is 'not the same as a "guessing penalty," such as the one imposed on the SAT Suite tests administered prior to the 2015–2016 academic year, which operated on a question-by-question basis.' But the model DOES factor guessing in: scoring is a function of '(3) whether a student's response pattern across questions suggests guessing,' and 'Random guessing or choosing (for example) option A for all multiple-choice questions... is unlikely to benefit their scores.' College Board's own advice is to eliminate one or two options first; the Student Guide says 'for most students, it's better to guess than leave a question blank, especially if you can eliminate' options. Say 'educated guessing beats blanks' rather than 'no penalty, so never leave a blank.' A related consequence the brief should note: because of IRT, 'two students may obtain the same number of correct responses on two different test forms but still have different reported scale scores.' Sources: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/assessment-framework-for-digital-sat-suite.pdf ; https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/sat-student-guide.pdf

corrections.original_claim: Every question in module 1 carries routing weight in addition to its own score contribution
corrections.correction: Not supported as stated. Two of module 1's 27 (RW) or 22 (Math) questions are pretest and by definition contribute nothing to the score — the Framework says 'Answers to pretest questions do not contribute in any way to students' Reading and Writing section score.' Whether pretest responses feed the routing decision is not published anywhere in v3.01. The defensible version of the point is the brief's own practical framing, which survives intact: because pretest items are indistinguishable, a student cannot know which questions count, so treating every question as scored is the correct behavior. Source: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/assessment-framework-for-digital-sat-suite.pdf

corrections.original_claim: [Omission check] Nothing in the brief describes the pre-2024 paper SAT
corrections.correction: No paper-SAT contamination found. The brief contains no essay section, no separate no-calculator Math section, no long-passage question sets, and no 3-hour timing — all correct. The Framework confirms the discrete-question design as a deliberate break from paper: 'All questions on the digital SAT Suite are in a discrete (standalone) format... This represents a departure from the paper-and-pencil SAT Suite, which used a combination of discrete questions and question sets.' One genuine omission to add: the brief presents the adaptive specs as universal, but a linear (nonadaptive) digital form exists for students approved for certain accommodations (human reader, raised line drawings, paper forms), and it 'has a slightly higher number of test questions in each module to account for the fact that the test is not adaptive' — specs in Framework Appendix E, practice available in Bluebook. So '98 questions, two-stage adaptive' is true for most students, not all. Sources: https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/assessment-framework-for-digital-sat-suite.pdf ; https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/sat-student-guide.pdf

corrections.original_claim: Required items on SAT test day (device, admission ticket, physical photo ID, pencils/pens, CB username+password; conditional wired non-Bluetooth headphones; EpiPens in clear bag under desk)
corrections.correction: All five items verified verbatim at https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/what-to-bring-do/what-to-bring, as is the EpiPen rule. Two additions: (a) CB's required bring-list also includes a sixth bullet the brief moved to 'optional' — 'An acceptable calculator for use on the Math section of the test (there will be an embedded calculator you can use within Bluebook…)'; (b) the what-to-bring page conditions the headphone requirement only on 'Text-to-Speech (Embedded)' — the 'or a screen reader' extension comes from the Proctor Manual prohibited-items note, not that page. Testing Rules §1 confirms 'You must bring your electronic or printed admission ticket,' so 'electronic accepted' is right.

corrections.original_claim: Optional items you may bring — including 'an acceptable handheld calculator, and backup calculator or batteries' as optional; under-desk list from the Fall 2026 Proctor Manual
corrections.correction: The under-desk list is verbatim correct (Proctor Manual p.26: power cord, portable charger, backup testing device, backup calculator or batteries, snack and drink, hand sanitizer/cleaning supplies), as is the Desmos toggle language (p.27). But CB's 'Nice to Have' list contains exactly five items — watch without an audible alarm, charging cable or portable charger, bag or backpack, drink or snacks, backup testing device. A handheld calculator is NOT in it; CB puts the calculator in the main bring-list. Sourcing caveat that applies to every Proctor Manual citation in this brief: the PDF currently served at satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/sats-proctor-manual.pdf is the Fall 2026 SAT Suite Proctor Manual for the IN-SCHOOL testing window (Oct 1–30, 2026). It contains zero occurrences of the word 'weekend' and describes a two-code check-in (5-letter room code + 6-digit start code) that does not match SAT Weekend. Most rules are shared, but weekend-specific procedure differs (see claims 12 and 13). Testing Rules §1 also allows an external mouse and mouse pad, which the brief omits.

corrections.original_claim: Prohibited items — 'exhaustive list' sourced to the prohibited-devices page
corrections.correction: Every item listed is genuinely prohibited, but the list is a merge of three sources presented as one page. The prohibited-devices page itself lists only: phones/smartwatches/fitness trackers/smart glasses/wearables; audio players and Bluetooth devices; detachable privacy screens; external keyboards for laptops or Chromebooks; 'Stylus for iPad'; cameras or recording devices; separate timers; notes/books/papers/reference materials; compasses/rulers/protractors/cutting devices; headphones/earbuds/earplugs; prohibited calculators; weapons and firearms. 'Stylus pens, Apple Pencils, smart pens,' 'dictionaries,' 'highlighters or colored pencils,' and 'papers of any kind' come from Testing Rules §2; 'scratch paper not provided by the proctor' and the hats/hoods rule come from the Proctor Manual (§Prohibited Items and §Behaviors, Testing Rules §3). The brief also drops CB's carve-outs: 'simple digital non-smartwatches or analog watches are acceptable,' 'keyboards for tablets are allowed,' and 'except your testing device or backup testing device.'

corrections.original_claim: Penalty for a prohibited device — exact CB framing quoted
corrections.correction: Both quotes verified verbatim (prohibited-devices page; Proctor Manual p.28 'Electronic Device Policies'), as is the device-collection language. One truncation: CB's sentence ends '…the device may be confiscated and its contents inspected.' The brief's quote stops at 'confiscated,' dropping the contents-inspection clause — which strengthens rather than weakens the point.

corrections.original_claim: Acceptable photo ID — the five criteria
corrections.correction: All five criteria verified at https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/what-to-bring-do/id-requirements.

corrections.original_claim: Acceptable and unacceptable ID documents, 21-and-older rule, testing outside home country
corrections.correction: Verified. Two small fixes: CB's unacceptable list names 'Missing Child ID cards,' not 'ChildFind cards'; and the stated exception to the passport requirement when testing outside your home country is a U.S. Department of War Common Access Card (CAC), which the brief omits. The country-specific exception list (Ghana, Hong Kong, Nepal, Nigeria, India, Pakistan, Jordan, Korea, Thailand, UAE, Vietnam) matches.

corrections.original_claim: Admission ticket — generated only after exam setup, available 5 days out
corrections.correction: Verified on both the Bluebook prepare-your-device page ('5 Days Before Test Day: Verification and Exam Setup') and what-to-bring ('available starting 5 days before the test'). CB's own FAQ phrases the window as '1–5 days before your test day.' Testing Rules §1 confirms 'Bluebook will generate your admission ticket once you have completed exam setup' and that electronic OR printed is acceptable. Students on a College Board–loaned device get the ticket on test day after setup.

corrections.original_claim: Device requirements — Windows 11 24H2, macOS 15, iPadOS 18, ChromeOS 144; 1 GB free (250 MB iPad); 3-hour battery for SAT Suite; Chromebook verified mode; mice always allowed; no external keyboards with laptops; no phones; VMs prohibited
corrections.correction: All verified verbatim at https://bluebook.collegeboard.org/technology/devices/requirements/overview. 'You cannot test on a mobile phone' is independently confirmed as a verbatim sentence in Testing Rules §1.

corrections.original_claim: Test-day-morning device checklist (7 steps) and 'close all applications other than Bluebook'
corrections.correction: The seven steps are verbatim from the Bluebook prepare-a-personal-device page. The application rule is verbatim Testing Rules §1: 'Close all applications other than Bluebook before the Test begins… You are not allowed to paste work into Bluebook from another program or application.'

corrections.original_claim: Charging and power during the test — clock doesn't stop, allowed vs. not-allowed lists
corrections.correction: Verified verbatim in the Proctor Manual (p.33–34, 'Access to Electricity'), including 'The testing clock won't stop, so students should continue to test while their device charges,' the three allowed options, the three not-allowed options, and the break-time low-battery watch instruction. Worth adding: 'Students approved to test with extended time must receive access to power when they need it,' and CB elsewhere warns it can't guarantee outlet access.

corrections.original_claim: If the device dies or crashes mid-test — the test DOES resume (timer pause, fix order, Let Student Continue Testing, device swap, 5-answer rule, never swap after time runs out)
corrections.correction: Every element verified verbatim in the Proctor Manual (p.40, 'A Student's Testing Is Interrupted'; 'How to Perform a Bluebook Device Swap'; p.31 'Exiting the test, closing laptops, and covering tablets can lead to incomplete answer submission and delayed scores or retesting'). The 'more than 5 answers → retest irregularity (Device swap issue IR)' rule is exact.

corrections.original_claim: Reporting time vs. start time — doors 7:45/8:00, 15–30 min check-in, start 8:15–8:30, end times, late arrivals sent to a late-testing room
corrections.correction: The published schedule is verified exactly (7:15 loaned-device arrivals, 7:45 check-in, 8:00 doors close, 8:15–8:30 testing starts, 10:45–11:00 standard, noon–12:15 time-and-a-half, 1:00–1:15 double time), as is 'You can't be admitted once testing has started,' assigned seating, Wi-Fi + start code, and 'The proctor can answer questions only about procedure.' Two problems: (1) 'Room check-in takes roughly 15–30 minutes' is nowhere published — it's an inference from the 7:45–8:15 gap; mark UNVERIFIED. (2) The late-testing-room instruction is in-school Proctor Manual guidance ('If students arrive after you start reading the script, send them to the late testing room (if available)'). The SAT Weekend student-facing rule is harsher and should be what a weekend test-taker is told: 'If you're late or absent on test day, you'll need to register again, and the standard testing fees will apply.'

corrections.original_claim: The 10-minute break — Bluebook times it, can't start/end early, staggered, 20-min nutrition break for some extended-time students
corrections.correction: All mechanics verified — help-center break page and Proctor Manual p.31 verbatim: 'Bluebook ends each section when time is up and displays break instructions. Students can't start or end scheduled breaks early. When their break time ends, students click a button to start the next section; no proctor action or instruction is needed.' The 20-minute nutrition break applies to students approved for extended time on the whole test (double time on the entire test also listed). Note the help-center page itself does not state the 10-minute length or the leave-the-room rule; those come from what-to-expect and the Proctor Manual.

corrections.original_claim: What you MAY and MAY NOT do during the break — quoted as 'SAT Weekend students can leave the room without asking the proctor to dismiss them' from the Proctor Manual
corrections.correction: The substance is right but that quoted sentence does not exist in the cited PDF — the Fall 2026 Proctor Manual contains no instance of the word 'weekend.' The official weekend support is the Test Day Experience page: 'When the first section ends, students are shown a break screen and told they can leave the room' and 'The proctor doesn't time the test or dismiss students at break.' The rest checks out from the correct sources: snack-and-drink-only and 'Students who leave the room for unscheduled breaks shouldn't take anything with them' (Proctor Manual p.31); the six break violations proctors watch for (p.31, verbatim); 'go to a locker at any time during the Test or breaks' and 'leave the testing room after you are finished without being dismissed by staff' (Testing Rules §3, not the manual); unscheduled breaks cost testing time and only 'breaks as needed' gets a Pause button (both confirmed). Two omissions worth adding: 'If you brought a calculator, it must remain on your desk during breaks,' and your ID 'will be checked every time you enter the testing room.'

corrections.original_claim: You must stay for the full standard time and cannot submit early
corrections.correction: Verbatim Testing Rules §1. The Proctor Manual independently confirms proctors are told to hold dismissal until time is up for all standard-time students, and that extended-time students may end early by choice. Add the adjacent Testing Rules sentence, which is the operational half of this: 'Do not close the lid or cover the screen of your testing device until your answers are submitted.'

corrections.original_claim: Test security agreement — what you agree not to do with test content (memorizing questions to write down later, AI tools, etc.)
corrections.correction: Every quoted phrase verified in Testing Rules §3 (revised May 19, 2026), including 'copy or record Test questions, memorize questions for the purpose of writing them down later, or take a screenshot during the Test' and 'AI tools such as ChatGPT, Photomath, and similar apps.' The 'unfair advantage… including through cyber or digital methods' sentence is verbatim from the Rules' introduction. The unfair-advantage examples (impersonation, switching devices or seats without permission, possessing answer keys, testing twice in a window without an approved retest) are verbatim Proctor Manual p.27.

corrections.original_claim: Penalties for violating the test security agreement
corrections.correction: Disciplinary Measures list is verbatim §5 (plus one item the brief drops: 'and share information with others as set forth in Section 5d'). One precision fix: the brief says future-test bans apply 'for deliberate violations.' The Rules condition Consequences on College Board finding 'substantial evidence you violated or attempted to violate these Rules, OR if scores from more than one College Board test administration (including SAT, AP, or CLEP) are found invalid' — the second trigger requires no finding of deliberateness. Also unmentioned: a 20-business-day Notice to Appeal window, and special voluntary-cancel/retest options for test takers in New York and California.

corrections.original_claim: Voluntary score cancellation — 11:59 p.m. ET one week after test date; cannot be submitted by phone or email; School Day uses a 5-day Test Day Toolkit form
corrections.correction: Deadline, irreversibility, and the School Day five-day Test Day Toolkit path all verified. But 'Cancellation requests cannot be submitted by phone or email' does not appear on the current page — that is a leftover from the pre-digital paper-SAT cancellation policy and should be dropped or marked UNVERIFIED. The current published process is: mysat.collegeboard.org → sign in → find the administration under My Scores → 'Unsure about scores?' → agree to the Cancellation of SAT Scores Agreement. CB adds 'You can cancel your score as soon as you leave the test center.'

corrections.original_claim: If answers don't submit because of an internet problem — two official pages disagree on the deadline
corrections.correction: The conflict is real and correctly characterized. Testing Rules §1: '11:59 p.m. local time the next day.' Bluebook fix-answer-submission-issues-sat-weekend: 'You have until two days after the test to submit your answers,' plus 'If any answers remain unsubmitted after two days, College Board will score your exam using the answers we received during testing.' A third CB page (what-to-expect) sides with the stricter reading twice: 'You must resubmit by the end of the following day.' That makes 2-to-1 for next-day, so the brief's operative-limit advice is sound.

corrections.original_claim: Technical problems during the test — raise your hand, proctor-mediated recovery, help room, start-code fix order, support lines 866-630-9305 / +1-212-713-8000
corrections.correction: The four-step start-code fix order and the help-room fallback are verbatim Proctor Manual p.40. The phone numbers are correct but are NOT in the Proctor Manual — they are published on CB's Contact Us and the Bluebook 'How can I contact Customer Support?' page (866-630-9305 U.S., +1 212-713-8000 international, 7:30 a.m.–8 p.m. ET). One omission that matters for a student who had a bad test day: test-day complaints must reach College Board by 11:59 p.m. ET on the 4th weekday after the administration (sat.org/testdaycomplaints).

corrections.original_claim: How to get a makeup test; in-school retests via IR; 2 retest opportunities; March 8, 2026 incident remedy
corrections.correction: Makeup-test page verified verbatim (CB contacts you; the two trigger conditions; the four requirements if selected). Retest policy verified in Proctor Manual pp.43–44: retest scenarios (fire alarms, technical issues after start and before time ran out, sickness after start, misadministrations), non-retest scenarios (answer submission errors, absentees, rule violations), 'Each student has only 2 opportunities to retest as a result of irregularities,' 'When students retest, they retake the entire assessment,' and the initial score held 'until the last published score release date.' The March 8, 2026 remedy is confirmed by College Board's own newsroom post: refund of registration fees plus a free future-SAT voucher, a March 14 score preview, and a March 22 makeup where available. Customer service 866-756-7346 / +1-212-713-7789 and sat.org/inquiry are correct.

corrections.original_claim: Score release timeline — '2–4 weeks' plus the Fall 2026 published dates
corrections.correction: Both the '2–4 weeks' line and all five date pairs (Aug 22→Sept 4; Sept 12→Sept 25; Oct 3→Oct 16; Nov 7→Nov 20; Dec 5→Dec 18) match https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/scores/score-release-dates exactly. studentscores.collegeboard.org is the correct student score-report portal, and sending scores to colleges is confirmed as a separate student-initiated action.

corrections.original_claim: Prohibited calculators — CAS models, QWERTY, wireless, cameras, tablets, pen-input, phone apps, paper tape; no cords; covers/backups under desk; delete documents, mute sound, tape IR ports, delete algebra programs
corrections.correction: This is the most precisely accurate claim in the brief. Every model family and every pre-test requirement is verbatim from Proctor Manual pp.27–28, including the carve-out 'Note that TI-Nspire models that do not include "CAS" in the name are acceptable' and '4-function calculators are not recommended.' One addition: students with raised or enlarged displays may be reseated at the test coordinator's discretion.

corrections.original_claim: Date-specific note: Aug. 23, 2026 Sunday administration and its score release are UNVERIFIED
corrections.correction: August 23, 2026 IS a published College Board Sunday test date. The Help Center page 'What Sunday dates are available?' lists, for fall 2026: August 23, September 20, October 18, November 8, and December 6, 2026 — note that the September Sunday is Sept 20, not the day after the Sept 12 Saturday, because CB skips Sundays that fall on religious holidays. Sunday testing is available only to students who cannot test Saturday for religious observance, and requires a letter from a religious leader on organizational stationery submitted via Customer Service (Registration → Change Saturday/Sunday status). What genuinely remains unverified is narrower: College Board publishes no separate score-release date for Sunday administrations, so the Sept 4, 2026 release tied to the Aug 22 Saturday date cannot be confirmed to apply to the Aug 23 Sunday sitting. The 'check your Bluebook admission ticket' advice is still correct.

corrections.original_claim: Gaps I could not verify (battery death, late return from scheduled break, confidentiality duration, submission-deadline conflict)
corrections.correction: Gaps (1), (3), and (4) hold up — I found no CB page quantifying the timer-pause window, no time limit on the confidentiality obligation in Testing Rules §3, and the submission-deadline conflict is real (and actually 2-to-1 in favor of next-day). Gap (2) is close to answerable from published mechanics: Bluebook times the break and the next section's timer starts only when the student clicks to begin it, so a late return does not consume section time — though the Proctor Manual does list 'returning late from break' among the behaviors proctors must watch for and report. The gap list should have named the biggest one: the 'Fall 2026 Proctor Manual' cited throughout is the in-school edition (testing window October 1–30, 2026), not an SAT Weekend document.

corrections.original_claim: Overall check for outdated pre-2024 paper-SAT content
corrections.correction: No paper-SAT contamination. Nothing in the brief references an essay section, a no-calculator math section, long multi-question passages, or a 3-hour test. The structural facts it does assert are current and correct: two sections (Reading and Writing, then Math), two separately timed modules each, one 10-minute break between sections, ~2h14m of testing, an embedded Desmos calculator, adaptive module structure ('Once you've moved on from a module, you cannot go back to it'). The extracted Proctor Manual text contains zero occurrences of 'essay' or 'no-calculator.' The one stale artifact I found is the 'no cancellation by phone or email' line in claim 17.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 5: 'College Board names only two testing points and describes their scope in prose... This is the authoritative boundary of what can be tested' — and Claim 6: 'College Board does not enumerate rules; this list is the prep-community synthesis.'
corrections.correction: College Board DOES enumerate the Standard English Conventions rule set officially. Assessment Framework, Appendix B, Table A33 'Digital SAT Suite Reading and Writing Section Skill/Knowledge Testing Points' (p.185 of https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/assessment-framework-for-digital-sat-suite.pdf) breaks both testing points into named sub-elements: BOUNDARIES -> 'Between Sentences' ('use contextually appropriate punctuation to properly mark the end of a sentence') and 'Within Sentences' ('coordinate clauses within a sentence or elements in a series using appropriate punctuation and, in some cases, a conjunction or conjunctive adverb; incorporate supplementary information (e.g., appositives, parentheticals) using appropriate punctuation; and recognize circumstances in which no punctuation is needed to set off sentence elements'). FORM, STRUCTURE, AND SENSE -> six named elements: Subject-Verb Agreement; Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement; Verb Finiteness ('verbs and verbals (i.e., gerunds, participles, infinitives)'); Verb Tense and Aspect; Subject-Modifier Placement; Genitives and Plurals ('choices among singular, plural, singular possessive, and plural possessive nouns and pronouns and among possessive determiners (its, their, your), contractions (it's, they're, you're), and adverbs (there)'). The brief's rule list should be re-labeled 'official' for items 1-3, 5-9, 11-13, 15-16, not 'reputable'.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 6, rule #9 Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement, presented as part of an unofficial 'prep-community synthesis'
corrections.correction: Understated, not wrong. 'Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement — Students will ensure agreement in number between a pronoun and its antecedent' is a named official element in Assessment Framework Appendix B, Table A33. This is officially in scope, not prep folklore.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 6, rule #14 PARALLELISM, listed with no hedge alongside officially-documented rules
corrections.correction: Parallelism is NOT named anywhere in College Board's official scope material: not in the Chapter 5 Standard English Conventions prose, not in Appendix B Table A33's six Form/Structure/Sense elements, and not in any of the seven Standard English Conventions performance-band descriptors in Skills Insight (Table 9, https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/skills-insight-digital-sat-suite.pdf). It deserves the same 'carried over from the paper SAT, treat as lower priority' hedge the brief correctly applied to illogical comparisons, who/whom, and pronoun case. Same applies to rule #10 (pronoun ambiguity), which the brief did hedge correctly.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 12: 'skillsinsight.pdf ... downloaded but not needed for these questions; it describes score-band performance descriptors rather than structure.'
corrections.correction: Skills Insight is a missed official corroborating source for the grammar section. Its Table 9 (Standard English Conventions, bands 1-7) names specific conventions and, in several cases, states the brief's traps in College Board's own words: 'Recognize when no punctuation should be used between a preposition and its object' (band 1); 'Eliminate unnecessary punctuation in challenging situations (e.g., between a long subject and its predicate...)' (band 5); 'Use a semicolon to mark the boundary between two closely related independent clauses when the clauses are joined by a conjunctive adverb (e.g., "however")' (band 6) — that is the brief's #1 comma-splice trap, officially confirmed; 'Establish logical agreement between a subject and a modifying element ... ensuring that an introductory modifier applies to its logical subject' (band 5); 'Determine when the possessive and/or plural form of a singular noun is required' (band 3); 'Properly incorporate restrictive and nonrestrictive sentence elements' (band 7). Notably, these bands contain zero mentions of pronouns, parallelism, or illogical comparisons.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 9: 'Words in Context ... (Assessment Framework, Table 11)' and Claim 10: 'Cross-Text Connections ... (Assessment Framework, Table 11)'
corrections.correction: Wrong table number. Table 11 is the Information and Ideas domain. Words in Context and Cross-Text Connections are in Table 12 (Craft and Structure). The quoted definitions themselves are verbatim correct; only the citation is off. Transitions and Rhetorical Synthesis at Table 13 (Expression of Ideas) are cited correctly — though strictly the definitions sit in the prose immediately following each table, not inside it.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 1: domain weights 'identical figures repeat in the Assessment Framework, Tables 11–14'
corrections.correction: Accurate but incompletely cited. Tables 11-14 each carry a 'Proportion' row repeating the figures, so the statement holds. However the canonical consolidated table is Table 10, 'Digital SAT Suite Reading and Writing Section Content Domains and Operational Question Distribution' — that is the cite to use.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 3 labeled confidence 'official', including consequences (b) 'Text 1 / Text 2 mark the end of Craft and Structure' and (d) 'The last few questions of the module are the hardest Rhetorical Synthesis items'
corrections.correction: The domain-level sequence (Table 9) and the ordering rule are genuinely official and verified verbatim. But (b) and (d) depend on WITHIN-domain skill order, which College Board explicitly does not publish — the framework says only that questions are 'ordered first by skill/knowledge element' without naming the elements' order. These two consequences belong in the 'reputable' claim, not the 'official' one. Extra caution: College Board's own Tables 10 and 13 list Rhetorical Synthesis BEFORE Transitions — the opposite of the brief's claimed appearance order — so CB table ordering is not evidence of sequence in either direction, and the brief should not be read as having official backing for Rhetorical Synthesis coming last.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 8: Rhetorical Synthesis items 'are ALWAYS the last questions of each module — the officially hardest items you will face.'
corrections.correction: 'Officially' is wrong. What is official is that Expression of Ideas is the last domain block and that questions within a block run easiest-to-hardest. That Rhetorical Synthesis specifically closes the block is a prep-source observation (Test Innovators: 'you will always start a module with the easiest "words in context" question and finish with the hardest "rhetorical synthesis" question'), corroborated by released practice tests but never published by College Board. Downgrade to 'reputable'.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 8: 'every choice is factually accurate and drawn from the notes. Truth is not the discriminator. Only goal-fulfillment is.'
corrections.correction: Contradicted by the brief's own wrong-answer list two paragraphs later ('INVENTS INFORMATION — slips in a causal claim where the notes showed only correlation'). Both cannot be true. The cited source (prepmaven.com/blog/test-prep/sat-rhetorical-synthesis-strategy/) does not make the 'every choice is accurate' claim; it says only that 'you can almost always find the correct answer choice without even looking at the bullet points.' Soften to: goal-fulfillment is the primary discriminator, but a minority of distractors do misstate or overreach the notes, so a finalist should still be checked against them.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 9: Words in Context questions are first in each module, 'meaning they are also, by the ordering rule, among the easiest questions you will see.'
corrections.correction: Internally inconsistent with the brief's own correct sawtooth point (claim 3a). Difficulty resets at the start of every skill group, so only the FIRST Words in Context item is guaranteed easy; the tail of the Words in Context block contains the hardest items of that type. The block as a whole is not 'among the easiest questions you will see.' The brief's very next sentence ('the last two or three in the block are where 600-750 students actually lose points') is the correct framing.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 10: 'another prep source claims 2–3 [Cross-Text Connections] per module'
corrections.correction: I could not locate a 2-3-per-module figure at the cited source. PrepMaven's cross-text article states 'you'll often see only one of these questions per module' (~2 per test). PrepScholar's measured average across six official practice tests is exactly 1.0 per test (1.9%). The brief's practical advice ('plan for one or two') is sound; the characterization of the conflicting source is not supported.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 4: PrepScholar per-type counts (Words in Context ~10–11, Transitions ~5–6, Rhetorical Synthesis ~5–6, Boundaries ~5–6, Form/Structure/Sense ~7–8, etc.)
corrections.correction: Matches PrepScholar's published table (blog.prepscholar.com/breakdown-of-every-question-type-in-sat-reading-by-percentage), averaged over six official practice digital SATs: Words in Context 10.6 (19.6%), Form/Structure/Sense 7.8, Transitions 5.6, Rhetorical Synthesis 5.6, Boundaries 5.6, Central Ideas and Details 4.6, Command of Evidence textual 4.0, Command of Evidence quantitative 3.6, Inferences 3.6, Text Structure and Purpose 2.2, Cross-Text Connections 1.0. One caveat the brief omits: these percentages are computed against all 54 questions, so they include pretest items, whereas College Board's official percentages are against the 50 operational questions. Cross-Text Connections should read ~1, not ~1-2.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 4: the within-domain question-type sequence (Words in Context -> Text Structure and Purpose -> Cross-Text Connections -> Central Ideas and Details -> Command of Evidence -> Inferences -> [SEC interleaved] -> Transitions -> Rhetorical Synthesis), and the Test Innovators quote
corrections.correction: The Test Innovators quote is verbatim accurate ('The testing points always appear in the same order, and the questions within each testing point are presented in order of increasing difficulty'), as is the endpoints claim. The full 10-item sequence is that article's presentation order rather than an explicitly numbered list it publishes — the brief's own caveat about Command of Evidence vs. Inferences is appropriately placed, and the same 'presentation order, not stated order' caveat should extend to items 1-3 as well. The reputable/not-official labeling is correct.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 2: 54 questions (25 operational + 2 pretest per module), two 32-minute modules, 64 minutes, 1.19 min/question, two-stage adaptive with a routing Module 1, discrete four-option MC with no shared-passage sets, 25–150 word passages, tables/bar/line graphs only, grade bands 6–8/9–11/12–14, 200–800, free navigation within a module but no return across modules, and 'all the information needed to answer each question is provided in the passage or passages themselves'
corrections.correction: Every element verified verbatim against Assessment Framework Table 8 and sections 3.1.1, 3.1.2, 3.1.6 (pp. 49-51) and section 2.2.5 ('All questions on the digital SAT Suite are in a discrete (standalone) format'; 'no question is linked to any other question in the section'). No paper-SAT contamination anywhere in the brief: no essay, no no-calculator section, no long passages with question sets, no 3-hour length.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 3: Table 9 domain sequence (Craft and Structure -> Information and Ideas -> Standard English Conventions -> Expression of Ideas, identical in both modules), the within-block ordering rule, the pretest-placement sentence, and the Specifications Overview prose
corrections.correction: All four quoted passages are verbatim correct, verified against the live PDFs. Assessment Framework p.50 Table 9 and the paragraph on p.51; Specifications Overview p.13 (printed page 12) for the prose sentence and p.14 (printed 13) for Table 2. Claim 1's domain weights, question-count ranges, testing points, and the four verbatim domain definitions are all confirmed exactly, as is the operational-vs-total note (28/26/26/20 of 50 = 14/13/13/10, summing to 100%).

corrections.original_claim: Claim 5: the official Boundaries and Form/Structure/Sense scope prose, the 'no punctuation' sample question, and the dangling-modifier sample question
