corrections.correction: All verbatim correct. Chapter 5, section 5.2.1.5 (pp.139-140) carries both scope passages exactly as quoted. The sample Boundaries item (Nakayama/dandelion) has key D with the explanation 'No punctuation is needed' and distractors A/B/C 'each inserts unnecessary punctuation (a comma, colon, and semicolon, respectively) between the sentence's subject ... and the verb.' The sample Form/Structure/Sense item (Rabinal Achi) has key A, with 'all these choices result in dangling modifiers.' These are College Board's own published illustrative samples, not recalled items. One nuance: College Board's phrasing is illustrative, not exhaustive ('address such matters as', 'such as'), so 'the authoritative boundary of what can be tested' overstates it even setting aside the Appendix B enumeration.

corrections.original_claim: Claim 11: the public College Board HTML page content, and Claim 12: provenance of the local PDF extracts
corrections.correction: The HTML page (satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/whats-on-the-test/reading-writing) carries the four domain descriptions, 'each of which includes questions from all four different domains,' and 'questions that test similar skills and knowledge are grouped together and arranged from easiest to hardest' — and, as the brief correctly notes, no percentage weights and no domain sequence. On provenance: I re-downloaded both PDFs and they are MD5-identical to the local copies (framework dc9c1009..., spec 0d4f46c9...), so the local extracts are genuine. The unrelated pt11.pdf in that directory is College Board's official 'SAT Practice Test #11' paper-accommodation edition (PDF metadata author: College Board), i.e. published practice material, not a leaked administration.

result.summary:
I researched only published, official structure and legitimate strategy material. No recalled/leaked items, no r/SAT, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram or Discord, and nothing about any specific administration. Sources are College Board (structure page, calculator policy, adaptive-testing blog, scoring page, Bluebook tools page, the official Bluebook Test Directions PDF, and the 239-page Digital SAT Suite Technical Manual), Desmos Studio's own help center and its SY2026-27 College Board configuration PDF, Khan Academy's Official SAT Practice articles (College Board's official practice partner), and reputable commercial prep (Target Test Prep, PrepScholar, Princeton Review). For section A I went further than reading about it: I loaded the actual College Board build of the calculator at desmos.com/testing/collegeboard/graphing and executed each play, so the syntax below is verified against the exact tool that ships in Bluebook, not against public Desmos.

The highest-value single finding for Desmos is that the College Board build accepts a one-variable equation typed verbatim — no rearranging, no "graph both sides" — and draws a vertical line at every solution whose x-intercept you click to read the answer (verified: typing 3x+7=x-5 produced a vertical line whose point of interest reads (-6, 0); a rational equation produced one vertical line per root). Same for a circle in general form and for a line in standard form: type it as printed, it graphs. The tool's only documented differences from public Desmos are that images, folders, and notes are disabled and Log mode is auto-checked for regressions — I confirmed this by opening the Add Item menu, which offers only expression, table, and inference. On pacing, the officially documented facts that most change behavior are that Math items are ordered easiest-to-hardest across each module while Reading and Writing items are ordered by domain (Craft and Structure, Information and Ideas, Standard English Conventions, Expression of Ideas) with difficulty resetting inside each domain — so "later equals harder" is true in Math and false in R&W. On routing (part C), College Board publishes the mechanism but not the number: the technical manual states the cut score was set from the median of archival population data so roughly 50% route each way, and it is an IRT ability estimate, not a raw count. Every "you need 14/22" figure in circulation is an unofficial third-party estimate and I have labeled it as such.

claims.claim: The Bluebook Desmos graphing calculator differs from public Desmos in exactly two documented ways
claims.detail: Desmos Studio's own configuration sheet for College Board exams (marked 'Updated for SY2026-2027') states: the Four-Function and Scientific calculators 'do not differ from the ones on desmos.com'; for the Graphing Calculator, 'Images, folders, and notes are disabled on your test' and 'The calculator on your test automatically checks Log mode when working with applicable exponential, logarithmic, and power regressions.' Nothing else is removed. I verified this directly on the live College Board build: the '+' (Add Item) menu offers only three entries — expression, table, inference — with no image, folder, or note option. PRACTICE ON THE EXACT TOOL: https://www.desmos.com/testing/collegeboard/graphing (the header reads 'Graphing Calculator | College Board Version'). Practicing on public desmos.com is fine but the testing build is one click away and identical to test day.

claims.claim: PLAY 1 (highest leverage): type any one-variable equation verbatim — Desmos draws a vertical line at each solution
claims.detail: You do NOT need to rearrange, move everything to one side, or graph both sides as two functions. Type the equation exactly as printed. VERIFIED LIVE on the College Board build: typing `3x+7=x-5` drew a vertical line; clicking where it crosses the x-axis popped the label `(-6, 0)` — that is the solution. Typing `2/(x-3) = x/4` (entered as a stacked fraction) drew TWO vertical lines, one at each root, so 'how many solutions' is answered by counting lines. WHAT TO TYPE, key by key: type the left side, press the `=` key, type the right side. For fractions press `/` (Desmos builds a stacked fraction; press the right-arrow key to escape the denominator). For exponents press `^` then right-arrow to escape. Then click the line where it meets the x-axis, and click the gray dot again to pin the coordinate label on screen. This one move covers linear equations, rational equations, radical equations, absolute-value equations, and 'how many real solutions' questions.

claims.claim: PLAY 2: graph both sides and click the intersection — the fallback when Play 1 is awkward
claims.detail: Type `y=` then the left side on line 1, and `y=` then the right side on line 2. Desmos documents that 'When you graph an expression or equation, you will notice points of interest in gray on your graph... at intercepts, intersection points, maximums, and minimums.' To use them: click the curve (or its expression line) to select it, hover a gray dot to reveal its coordinates, click the dot to pin the label until you deselect. Equivalent single-line version: type `f(x)=` (left side) `-` (right side) and click the x-intercept — the zero of the difference is the solution. Use Play 2 over Play 1 when you also need to SEE the behavior (e.g. which of two quantities is larger over a range) rather than just get a number.

claims.claim: PLAY 3 (systems): type both equations in whatever form they are printed — no solving for y
claims.detail: VERIFIED LIVE: `2x+3y=12` graphs as a line immediately; Desmos handles implicit equations, so standard form, point-slope, and general form all work untouched. Type equation 1 on line 1, equation 2 on line 2, click either line, and click the gray intersection dot. Diagnostics you get for free: two parallel lines that never meet = 'no solution'; two lines that render as one = 'infinitely many solutions'; for a line-and-parabola system count the intersection dots. If the intersection is off-screen, use the wrench (Graph Settings, top right) to type explicit x-min/x-max/y-min/y-max bounds rather than pinch-zooming blindly.

claims.claim: PLAY 4 (quadratics): zeros and vertex are both points of interest — no factoring, no completing the square, no quadratic formula
claims.detail: Type the quadratic in whatever form it is printed: `y=2x^2-7x+3`, or `y=2(x-3)(x+1)`, or `y=3(x-4)^2-5`. Click the parabola. Gray points of interest appear at the x-intercepts (the zeros / roots / solutions), the y-intercept, and the vertex (a maximum or minimum). Click each to read exact coordinates. This directly answers: roots, sum or product of roots, the vertex, the axis of symmetry (the x-coordinate of the vertex), the maximum or minimum value (the y-coordinate), and the y-intercept — all from one typed line. Caution: read the QUESTION for which coordinate it wants; the single most common Desmos error is reading the x-coordinate when the question asked for the minimum VALUE (the y-coordinate).

claims.claim: PLAY 5 (sliders): 'for what value of k does this have exactly one solution' — type the letter and drag
claims.detail: Desmos documentation: 'adding a slider is as simple as typing a letter where you might normally see a number. Any time you have free variables in an expression, the calculator will prompt you to define them with sliders.' VERIFIED LIVE on the College Board build: typing `y=x^2+k` produced an `k=1` line with a play button and a slider bar defaulting to -10..10. WHAT TO TYPE: put the unknown constant in as a bare letter exactly where it appears (`y=x^2+bx+9`, `y=ax^2-4x+1`), click 'add slider' when prompted, then drag. Count intersection points as you drag: the value where two curves become tangent (intersections drop from 2 to 1 to 0) is the 'exactly one solution' answer. To read a precise slider value, click the number on the slider row and type bounds/step (e.g. step 0.01) instead of dragging by eye. Also use a slider to test 'for which value of c is the system inconsistent' and discriminant-style questions without touching b^2-4ac.

claims.claim: PLAY 6 (regression / line of best fit): table plus `y_1 ~ mx_1 + b`
claims.detail: Steps: click `+` (top left) then `table`. Type the x-values down the `x_1` column and the y-values down the `y_1` column (arrow keys move cell to cell). Then either click the 'Add Regression' button on the table, or start a NEW expression line and type `y_1 ~ mx_1 + b` — a TILDE, not an equals sign. Type the subscript with the underscore key: `y`, `_`, `1`, right-arrow to escape the subscript. Desmos's own note: 'the tilde is usually to the left of the 1 on most keyboards or in the bottom row of the ABC part of the Desmos keypad.' VERIFIED LIVE on the College Board build with 5 data points: the expression expanded to show REGRESSION PARAMETERS m = 1.96 and b = 0.14, STATISTICS R^2 = 0.9976 and r = 0.9988, plus a residuals 'plot' button. OTHER MODELS: exponential `y_1 ~ ab^{x_1}`; quadratic `y_1 ~ ax_1^2+bx_1+c`; the parameters are then stored as ordinary variables, so you can type `f(x)=1.96x+0.14`-style follow-ups, or just type `am+b`-style expressions, to predict a value the question asks for. Note Log mode is auto-checked on the test for exponential/log/power regressions.

claims.claim: PLAY 7 (backsolve): a function table tests all four answer choices at once
claims.detail: Define the function on one line: `f(x)=3x^2-5x-12`. Then click `+` then `table`. Leave the first column header as `x_1`, and in the SECOND column header type `f(x_1)` — Desmos then auto-computes the column. Type the four answer choices into the `x_1` column and read which one produces the target output. VERIFIED LIVE on the College Board build: with header `f(x_1)`, inputs -3, -2, 1, 3 auto-filled to 30, 10, -14, 0. Desmos documents this: 'If you put a function of x in the second header, the values will be calculated using the values in the first column.' You can add a THIRD column with a second function (`g(x_1)`) to compare two functions side by side on the same inputs. This turns any 'which value of x satisfies...' multiple-choice question into four keystrokes. A related shortcut: with an expression selected, 'Edit List' then 'Create Table' converts a function into a table of values automatically.

claims.claim: PLAY 8 (inequalities): type the inequality and Desmos shades the solution region
claims.detail: VERIFIED LIVE on the College Board build: typing `y>=-2x+4` shaded the correct half-plane. Type `>=` as `>` then `=` (Desmos converts it to the proper symbol), or use the on-screen keypad. For a SYSTEM of inequalities, type each on its own line; the overlap renders as the darker region. To test whether a specific point satisfies the system — which is what these questions usually ask — type the point itself, e.g. `(3,5)`, and see whether the plotted dot lands inside the darker overlap. That is faster and less error-prone than substituting into both inequalities by hand. For constrained word problems, add `x>=0` and `y>=0` to trim the region to the first quadrant.

claims.claim: PLAY 9 (circles): type the general form verbatim, then click the top and bottom points of interest
claims.detail: You do not need to complete the square. VERIFIED LIVE on the College Board build: typing `x^2+y^2-6x+4y-12=0` graphed the circle immediately; selecting the curve produced gray points of interest at its top and bottom; clicking the top point popped the label `(3, 3)` and the bottom gives `(3, -7)`. From those two points: the center is the midpoint, (3, -2), and the radius is half the vertical distance, 5. That answers center, radius, diameter, circumference, and area questions from one typed line. If the question gives center and radius and asks for the general form, do the reverse: type the candidate answer choices and see which one produces the described circle. Note the leftmost/rightmost points are not offered as points of interest on an implicit curve — use the top and bottom, which is sufficient.

claims.claim: Supporting syntax worth memorizing: restrictions, statistics functions, and the exact statistic Desmos computes
claims.detail: DOMAIN RESTRICTION: `y=2x{0<x<5}` graphs only that piece — type the braces with the `{` key. Useful for piecewise definitions and for trimming a model to a sensible domain in a word problem. STATISTICS, all VERIFIED LIVE on the College Board build with the list [1,2,3,4,10]: `mean([1,2,3,4,10])` = 4; `median(...)` = 3; `stdev(...)` = 3.53553390593; `quartile([1,2,3,4,10],1)` = 1.5; `total(...)` sums the list. IMPORTANT TRAP: `stdev` is the SAMPLE standard deviation (divides by n-1); the population version is `stdevp`. Type a list with square brackets and commas. Also verified: `sqrt(40)` = 6.32455532034 and `2/3` = 0.666666666667 — which feeds directly into the SPR entry rules below.

claims.claim: Both Desmos calculators are available on every Math question, and their contents do NOT carry over between them
claims.detail: College Board: 'Bluebook contains an embedded Desmos calculator with two options—graphing or scientific. Students can toggle between the two.' There is no no-calculator portion; the calculator is available for all 44 Math questions and is not available in Reading and Writing. Desmos's FAQ adds a practical warning: 'You can toggle between each calculator during the exam. However, content in one calculator won't carry over to content in the other calculator, so double-check that you've toggled into the correct calculator before inputting anything.' Practical implication: pick ONE (the graphing calculator does everything the scientific one does) and stay in it, so you never lose typed work by toggling. You may also bring an approved handheld as a backup; CAS calculators are prohibited.

claims.claim: HARD LIMIT: Desmos is not a CAS — it will not factor, simplify, expand, or solve symbolically
claims.detail: Desmos states plainly: 'No. Desmos is not considered a computer algebra system (CAS), which is recognized by its ability to solve equations algebraically, simplify expressions, and perform exact arithmetic without rounding or truncating decimals. While Desmos can quickly evaluate expressions, plot, and graph, students must be able to analyze and interpret the outputs.' Concretely, Desmos cannot: factor a polynomial for you, expand a binomial symbolically, simplify a rational expression, solve a literal equation for one variable in terms of others, return an exact radical or exact fraction as the answer to an equation, or do matrix operations. Every question whose ANSWER CHOICES ARE EXPRESSIONS rather than numbers is outside Desmos's reach as a direct solver — the best it can do there is a graphical equivalence check (see next claim).

claims.claim: The equivalence-check workaround, and why it is not proof
claims.detail: For 'which expression is equivalent to' questions you can type `y=` the given expression and `y=` a candidate answer choice and see whether the two graphs coincide. This works, but it has real failure modes to know: (1) two graphs can coincide over the visible window and differ outside it, so it is visual evidence, not proof; (2) removable discontinuities (holes) from cancelled factors are invisible at default zoom, so a rational expression and its 'simplified' version look identical when they are technically not equal at the excluded x-value; (3) checking four choices means typing four extra lines, which is often slower than recognizing the factorization. Use it as a confirmation of an algebraic hunch, or as a last resort when you are stuck, not as the first move.

claims.claim: Where reaching for Desmos is actively SLOWER than algebra — the do-not-open list
claims.detail: Prep sources converge on this, and it matches the CAS limitation above. Do NOT open Desmos for: (1) anything you can finish in under ~15 seconds by hand — typing a long expression costs 30-45 seconds; (2) questions whose answer choices are algebraic expressions, not numbers (nothing to graph); (3) plug-in / evaluate-a-function questions where you already have the value (`f(3)` typed into Desmos is slower than mental arithmetic on a simple polynomial); (4) plane geometry that is not on a coordinate grid — angle chasing, similar triangles, arc length, volume: use the on-screen Reference Sheet instead; (5) statistical-reasoning questions (margin of error, sampling method, correlation vs causation, effect of an outlier on mean vs median) — these are pure reasoning; (6) interpret-the-slope-or-intercept-in-context questions, which are reading questions; (7) three-variable systems, since the graphing calculator here is 2D; (8) ratio, percent, and unit-conversion word problems. The rule that scales: Desmos earns its 30 seconds only when the graph, intersection, zero, or table IS the mathematics the question is asking for.

claims.claim: TRAP: Desmos returns long decimals, and the official student-produced-response entry rules will reject a naive rounding
claims.detail: Verbatim from the official Bluebook Test Directions: 'You can enter up to 5 characters for a positive answer and up to 6 characters (including the negative sign) for a negative answer. If your answer is a fraction that doesn't fit in the provided space, enter the decimal equivalent. If your answer is a decimal that doesn't fit in the provided space, enter it by truncating or rounding at the fourth digit. If your answer is a mixed number (such as 3 1/2), enter it as an improper fraction (7/2) or its decimal equivalent (3.5). Don't enter symbols such as a percent sign, comma, or dollar sign.' College Board's own example table: for the answer 2/3, ACCEPTABLE entries are `2/3`, `.6666`, `.6667`, `0.666`, `0.667`; entries that will NOT receive credit are `0.66`, `.66`, `0.67`, `.67`. For -1/3: `-1/3`, `-.3333`, `-0.333` are acceptable; `-.33`, `-0.33` are not. This matters precisely because Desmos displays `0.666666666667` — copying the first two or three decimals is the natural move and it is wrong. Best habit: enter the exact fraction (`2/3`) whenever it fits, and only fall back to a four-digit decimal when it does not.

claims.claim: The on-screen Reference Sheet already contains the geometry formulas — do not waste Desmos time or memory on them
claims.detail: The official Bluebook directions reproduce the reference sheet available on every Math question: area of rectangle A = lw, area of triangle A = (1/2)bh, area of circle A = pi*r^2, circumference C = 2*pi*r, Pythagorean theorem c^2 = a^2 + b^2, volumes V = lwh, V = pi*r^2*h, V = (4/3)pi*r^3, V = (1/3)pi*r^2*h, V = (1/3)lwh, the two special right triangles (30-60-90 with sides x, x*sqrt(3), 2x; and 45-45-90 with sides s, s, s*sqrt(2)), plus '360 degrees of arc in a circle', '2*pi radians of arc in a circle', and 'the sum of the measures in degrees of the angles of a triangle is 180.' What is NOT on the sheet and must be known cold: the quadratic formula, slope, midpoint and distance formulas, exponent rules, the standard/general equation of a circle, SOHCAHTOA, and percent-change.

claims.claim: Official module structure, and the fact that 2 of the questions you see in every module do not count
claims.detail: From the College Board Technical Manual: Reading and Writing is 54 items in two 32-minute modules of 27; 'Of each module's 27 items, 25 are operational... and 2 items are pretest. Answers to pretest items do not contribute in any way to students' Reading and Writing section score.' Math is 44 items in two 35-minute modules of 22; 'Of each module's 22 items, 20 are operational... and 2 are pretest.' Average time per item is officially 1.19 minutes (about 71 seconds) for R&W and 1.59 minutes (about 95 seconds) for Math. Pretest items are indistinguishable from scored ones, so this is not something to game — but it is a real reason not to spiral over one impossible-looking question: there is a nonzero chance it is not even scored.

claims.claim: Math questions are officially ordered easiest to hardest across each module; Reading and Writing questions are NOT
claims.detail: This is the single most actionable pacing fact and it is officially documented. For Math: 'Items from all four content domains appear in each test module. Across each module, items are arranged from easiest to hardest, allowing each test taker the best opportunity to demonstrate what they know and can do.' For Reading and Writing the order is by DOMAIN, in this fixed sequence: Craft and Structure, then Information and Ideas, then Standard English Conventions, then Expression of Ideas. 'Within each content domain except Standard English Conventions, items are ordered first by skill/knowledge element and then by item difficulty from easiest to hardest. Standard English Conventions items are ordered from easiest to hardest irrespective of skill/knowledge element tested.' CONSEQUENCE: in Math, banking time early is correct and the questions you sacrifice should be at the END. In R&W, difficulty RESETS four times, so a brutal question is routinely followed by an easy one — never quit a R&W module because the last three were hard, and never assume question 25 is harder than question 12. Embedded pretest items sit alongside items testing the same skill, so they do not disturb the ordering logic.

claims.claim: You can move freely WITHIN a module, but a finished module is gone forever, and you cannot start module 2 early
claims.detail: Official Bluebook directions: 'Within each section, the two modules are timed separately. If time permits, you can review your answers in a given module. When the timer reaches zero, you will automatically move on. Once you move on from any module, you cannot return to it.' The technical manual adds that students may not return to the R&W section once Bluebook has moved them to Math. Khan Academy (College Board's official practice partner) makes the practical point explicit: 'On the real test, you won't be able to move onto the second module until your 32 minutes for the first module are up. On the practice tests, you can skip to the second module earlier, but we recommend against it... use any leftover time just like you would on the real test: to review the questions you're not sure about.' PRACTICE IMPLICATION: if you have been ending practice modules early, you have been training the wrong reflex. Finishing early is not a reward; it is 6 free minutes of review that you must learn to spend.

claims.claim: The official two-pass method, stated by College Board's own practice partner
claims.detail: Khan Academy's Official SAT Practice article on Math time management: 'Use the two passes strategy. With this technique, you'll go through each module once to answer all the questions that you feel confident about. Make sure to mark any questions you don't complete so you can come back to them during round two! After you've completed your first round and gotten all those easy points, head back to those skipped questions and get to work on them. This way, you prioritize spending time on the questions most likely to earn you points.' It also says: 'Don't second-guess yourself! Go with your gut... Your first instinct is usually correct'; and 'Leave time at the end of each module to review your answers. If you find yourself stumped on a question or stuck between two or more choices, just take your best guess and move on.'

claims.claim: The non-negotiable flagging rule: ANSWER FIRST, then flag — never flag an empty question
claims.detail: Khan Academy, verbatim in both the Math and the Reading and Writing time-management articles: 'Don't leave any questions blank! The SAT doesn't penalize you for wrong answers, so no matter how stumped you feel on a given question, you should always take a guess. You should select a choice the first time you encounter the question, even if you mark it to come back to later—just in case you run out of time before you get back to it.' Target Test Prep says the same thing independently: 'Even if you mark a question for later review, be sure to answer the question before you mark it for review. That way, if you run out of time before you have a chance to revisit it, you have a chance of getting it correct.' Mechanically: click an answer, THEN click the bookmark icon next to the question number, then advance. This single habit is the cheapest points on the test — it converts every question you run out of time on from a guaranteed 0 into a 25% shot.

claims.claim: No penalty for wrong answers — official, and the reason blanks are strictly dominated
claims.detail: College Board: 'Remember: there's no penalty for guessing. It's better to answer every question the best you can.' The SAT uses rights-only scoring. Expected value: a blind guess on a four-option multiple-choice question is worth 25%; eliminating one choice with the Option Eliminator raises it to about 33%; eliminating two raises it to 50%. Target Test Prep extends the rule to the fill-in questions: 'Don't leave any SPR (fill-in-the-blank) questions blank, either. Instead, choose a reasonable answer based on the question and go for it! For example, if the question asks how many solutions a particular equation has, pick a whole number like 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5.' A blank and a wrong answer score identically, so a blank is never correct — there is no scenario on this test where leaving something empty is the right play.

claims.claim: MATH CHECKPOINT SYSTEM: the '12 and 24' rule, with explicit recovery thresholds
claims.detail: Target Test Prep's published checkpoint for a 22-question, 35-minute Math module: 'when you are just starting question 12, your countdown clock should show 24 minutes remaining.' The logic is that because questions are ordered easiest to hardest, the first 11 should average about 1 minute each, banking time so that the remaining 11 get about 2 minutes 10 seconds each. RECOVERY TABLE: more than 24:00 left at Q12 = ahead, you have extra time for the hard tail. Between 18:00 and 22:00 = 'a bit behind your goal... but you're still okay. But you must work efficiently and not waste even a second on the rest of the module.' Below 17:30 = 'you have less time to answer the hard questions than it took you to answer the easier ones... it is likely that you will not finish. If this happens, spend time on the questions that you feel you can answer correctly. If you encounter an impossible question, make an educated guess, mark it for review, and move on.' Note 17:30 is exactly half the module time — the point at which you are on a flat pace and therefore behind, because the second half is harder.

claims.claim: READING AND WRITING CHECKPOINT SYSTEM: the '14 and 12' rule — deliberately front-loaded, and this is correct given the official item order
claims.detail: Target Test Prep's checkpoint for a 27-question, 32-minute R&W module: 'By the time you are about halfway through the module, just starting question 14, your countdown clock should read about 12 minutes.' The reasoning: 'It is reasonable to expect to spend about twice as much time answering each Reading passage question as each Writing question. Thus, you could plan an average of 1 1/2 minutes on each Reading passage and 45 seconds on each Writing question.' This looks backwards until you check it against the official item sequence — Craft and Structure and Information and Ideas (passage-based, reading-heavy) come FIRST, Standard English Conventions and Expression of Ideas (grammar, fast once you see the rule) come LAST. So spending 20 minutes on the first 13 and 12 minutes on the last 14 is the correct shape, not a mistake. TTP recommends using the same checkpoint in module 2. Sanity-check this against your own practice data before adopting it: TTP itself says 'you should get some digital SAT pacing practice by taking a few practice exams, to see if a given strategy works for you.'

claims.claim: The Bluebook tools, in College Board's exact words, and how each converts to a pacing action
claims.detail: From the official Bluebook students' tools page: 'Mark for Review: Use the bookmark icon to flag any question you want to come back to.' 'Option Eliminator: Cross out answer choices you think are wrong. You can undo this if you change your mind.' 'Highlights & Notes: Use this tool to highlight text from a question or leave yourself a note.' 'Line Reader: Use this tool to focus as you read test content.' 'Question Menu: See which questions you skipped or marked for review and navigate to any question in the section.' 'Testing Timer: A timer will let you know how much time is remaining in each part of the test' — and the technical manual adds it 'can, at students' discretion, be hidden until the five-minute mark in each test module.' 'Reference Sheet: A reference sheet with commonly used formulas will appear on all tests with math questions.' 'Zoom: Use keyboard shortcuts on laptops or pinch and zoom on tablets.' PACING ACTIONS: the Question Menu / end-of-module review page is your second pass — it lists exactly what you flagged. Hide the timer ONLY if it makes you panic; otherwise you need it for the checkpoints above. Use the Option Eliminator on every question you guess, because eliminating one choice takes your odds from 25% to 33%.

claims.claim: THE SACRIFICE STRATEGY, stated accurately: you sacrifice TIME, never the answer
claims.detail: No reputable source endorses leaving a question blank — the correct form of 'sacrificing' the hardest few is to pre-commit to spending ZERO solving time on them while still entering an answer. The mechanics: decide before you sit down how many questions per module you will abandon (a student targeting ~600 in a section can typically abandon 3-5 per module; a student targeting 750+ can abandon at most 1-2). When you hit one, immediately (a) click your Letter of the Day, (b) click the bookmark to flag it, (c) advance. Princeton Review's two named strategies here are Personal Order of Difficulty — 'work through easier questions and then circle back to more challenging ones' — and Letter of the Day, always guessing the SAME letter rather than choosing randomly, which removes a decision from a moment when you have no information. Two SAT-specific caveats: (1) because Math is ordered easiest to hardest, your sacrifices should cluster at the END of a Math module, but because R&W difficulty resets by domain, sacrifices in R&W must be chosen question-by-question, not positionally; (2) sacrifices in MODULE 1 are more expensive than in module 2, because module 1 both contributes half your scored items and determines routing.

claims.claim: The 'don't spiral' rules that protect the checkpoint system
claims.detail: Target Test Prep's test-day guidance, which is about protecting pace rather than content: 'Don't have a panic attack if you encounter a question that stresses you... Give it your best shot, use intelligent guessing, mark it for review, and move on.' 'If the first few questions just don't feel right, you may simply be taking a bit of time to adjust to the test... take a deep breath, make your best guess, mark the questions for review, and continue on!' 'During the SAT, you do not have the time or the energy to assess how well you're doing. This will distract you from the task at hand.' 'Don't spend an inordinate amount of time on any one question. You do NOT have to get every question correct to get a great score.' Practical translation: never let a single question consume more than roughly 2x your per-question budget (about 2.5 minutes in Math, about 2.5 minutes on a hard reading question) before you guess-flag-move.

claims.claim: PART C — OFFICIAL: the routing mechanism, and why a published number-correct threshold does not and cannot exist
claims.detail: The College Board Technical Manual documents a '1-2 design' multistage adaptive test: stage 1 is a single routing module of broad difficulty; 'Based on student performance on the initial module, Bluebook selects one of two potential second-stage modules to administer. One such module consists of a targeted mix of items that are, on average, of higher difficulty than those in the first module, while the other consists of a targeted mix of items that are, on average, of lower difficulty.' On how the cut is set: 'The SAT Suite of Assessments uses a population distribution approach to routing. This approach uses historic archive data of past student performance to determine the median student performance that is then used to set the routing decision point.' And, more explicitly: 'An alternative method is having around 50% of the exam population routed to either the lower- or higher-difficulty modules. To do this, College Board can use historical data to predict expectations for future ability distributions and set the cut score accordingly. In other words, College Board used the median test scores from archival data to set the cut score for the routing module.' THREE CONSEQUENCES: (1) the cut is an IRT ability (theta) estimate, not a raw number correct; (2) it is calibrated so roughly half of all test takers route each way; (3) because each panel is a differently-assembled set of items and 2 of the items you see are unscored pretest, no fixed 'X out of 22' can be true across forms. College Board has never published a raw-count threshold.

claims.claim: PART C — UNOFFICIAL ESTIMATE (label as such): third-party guesses at the raw-count routing threshold
claims.detail: MARK THIS CLEARLY AS AN UNOFFICIAL ESTIMATE — it is not a College Board figure and it varies by test form. Commercial prep sources converge loosely on roughly 60-70% correct in module 1. Target Test Prep, the most reputable source I found stating a number, says for Math: 'If you do well (getting about 13 or more of the 22 questions correct), then the second math module will present you with fewer easy questions and many medium and difficult (and score-enhancing) questions.' Other prep blogs put Math at roughly 14-15 of 22 and Reading and Writing at roughly 18-20 of 27. TTP also publishes an unofficial difficulty breakdown for Math module 1 (about 6 easy, 8 medium, 6 hard, plus 2 unscored) — College Board does not publish that mix either. PrepScholar, notably, declines to give a number and explains why: routing depends on 'the number of easy, average, and difficult questions that you answer correctly', i.e. the difficulty of what you got right, not a bare count — which is exactly consistent with the IRT mechanism in the technical manual. USABLE TAKEAWAY: treat ~65% correct in module 1 as a rough personal target for practice diagnostics, and treat any precise claim ('you need exactly 14') as folklore.

claims.claim: PART C — UNOFFICIAL: the 'score ceiling' claim, and how College Board's official language contradicts its framing
claims.detail: MARK AS UNOFFICIAL ESTIMATE. Prep sources widely claim that being routed to the lower-difficulty module 2 caps a section score somewhere in the high 500s to mid 600s even with a perfect module 2 (figures cited range from ~590 to ~650 per section). These figures appear to be inferred from Bluebook practice-test score reports, not from any College Board publication. College Board's official statements are deliberately different in framing: 'A range of section scores are possible no matter which second module a student sees'; 'Students won't be advantaged just for seeing a higher difficulty set of questions in the second module, or disadvantaged just for seeing a lower difficulty set of questions in the second module'; and 'Two students who answer the same number of questions correctly in a test section may earn differing section scores based on the characteristics, including difficulty level, of the particular questions they answered correctly.' The technical manual also states a design goal that 'it should be possible for all valid score points to be attained.' HOW TO USE THIS: do not tell a student 'if you get the easy module 2 you're capped at 590' as fact. The defensible, official version is the second-order point that follows: module 1 carries half your scored items AND sets your routing, so front-loaded effort and zero blanks in module 1 matter more than anywhere else on the test.

claims.claim: Desmos work persisting between questions and resetting between modules
claims.detail: MARK AS UNVERIFIED. Several prep sources state that within a module Desmos retains your typed expressions if you navigate away from a question and come back, but that it resets completely between module 1 and module 2. I could not find this in any College Board or Desmos official document, so treat it as a claim to confirm yourself on a Bluebook practice test rather than as fact. What IS officially documented and related: content does not carry over between the graphing and scientific calculators when you toggle between them, so pick one and stay in it. Practical habit regardless of persistence: delete lines you are finished with (click the X on the expression row) so a stale graph from a previous question never contaminates the one you are on — this is a real and common source of wrong answers.

claims.claim: One TTP claim I would NOT repeat to a student
claims.detail: Flagging this so it is not passed along uncritically. Target Test Prep writes: 'If you get even one lucky guess on a module 1 question, your total section score could be increased by as much as 200 points!' That is not supportable. A 200-point swing from a single item is inconsistent with the IRT scoring described in the technical manual, where the section score is computed from performance across all 40 (Math) or 50 (R&W) operational items in both modules. The kernel of truth is only that a module-1 item sits near the routing decision point and so carries somewhat more leverage than an average item. The honest version to tell a student: module 1 items are worth taking seriously twice over, but no single question is worth 200 points, and believing that will make you spend three minutes on question 7.

night_before_priorities: Drill the ONE Desmos move that covers the most questions: type any one-variable equation exactly as printed (e.g. 3x+7=x-5), let Desmos draw a vertical line at each solution, click where it crosses the x-axis, read the coordinate. Do 15 reps at https://www.desmos.com/testing/collegeboard/graphing so the keystrokes (/, ^, right-arrow to escape) are automatic. This subsumes linear, rational, radical, and absolute-value equations plus 'how many solutions'.

Lock in the answer-then-flag reflex: never advance past a question without a bubble filled in, even one you intend to return to. There is no wrong-answer penalty, so a blank is strictly worse than a guess in every case. Pair it with a pre-chosen Letter of the Day so guessing costs zero decision time.

Memorize the two checkpoints and nothing else about pacing: MATH — starting question 12, the clock should read 24:00 (below 17:30 means triage now). READING AND WRITING — starting question 14, the clock should read about 12:00 (front-loaded on purpose, because the reading questions come first and the fast grammar questions come last).

Internalize the official item ordering, because it determines which questions you sacrifice: Math is ordered easiest to hardest across the whole module, so bank time early and abandon at the END. R&W difficulty RESETS four times (Craft and Structure, Information and Ideas, Standard English Conventions, Expression of Ideas), so never quit a R&W module because the last few were brutal — the next domain starts easy again.

Practice the three points-of-interest reads until they are one motion: click the curve, then click the gray dot. Zeros and vertex on a parabola; intersection on a system; top-and-bottom on a circle typed in general form (x^2+y^2-6x+4y-12=0 gives (3,3) and (3,-7), so center (3,-2), radius 5). No factoring, no completing the square, no solving for y.

Rehearse the student-produced-response entry rules against a Desmos decimal, because this is a silent points-loser: 5 characters positive / 6 with a negative sign; enter the exact fraction when it fits; if you must use a decimal, truncate or round at the FOURTH digit. For 2/3, College Board accepts 2/3, .6666, .6667, 0.666, 0.667 and explicitly rejects 0.66, .66, 0.67, .67 — while Desmos shows 0.666666666667.

Learn the do-not-open list so Desmos does not cost you time: anything solvable in under 15 seconds by hand; questions whose answer choices are expressions rather than numbers; non-coordinate geometry (use the on-screen Reference Sheet); statistical-reasoning and interpret-the-slope questions; three-variable systems. Desmos is not a CAS — it will not factor, simplify, expand, or solve for a variable symbolically.

Set up regression and backsolve once tonight so you never have to think about the syntax: table via the + button, then either the Add Regression button or type y_1 ~ mx_1 + b (TILDE, left of the 1 key) to get m, b, r and R^2. Separately: define f(x)=..., add a table, put f(x_1) in the second column HEADER, and type the four answer choices into x_1 to test all of them at once.

Front-load module 1 of each section on purpose. It is officially half your scored items AND it sets the routing decision, whose cut College Board set at the population median. Every question you abandon in module 1 is more expensive than the same abandonment in module 2 — so if you are going to sacrifice, sacrifice later, not earlier.

On the practice test you take tonight or tomorrow morning, do NOT click into module 2 early — the real test will not let you. Train yourself to spend leftover minutes on the flagged questions in the review page, because on test day that time exists whether you use it or not.

Know the Bluebook tools cold so no test-day second is spent hunting: bookmark icon = Mark for Review, Option Eliminator for crossing out choices (25% to 33% odds), Highlights & Notes, Line Reader, the Question Menu (your second-pass checklist), the x^2 Reference Sheet icon, and the timer (hideable until the 5-minute mark if it makes you panic).

Pre-decide your sacrifice budget as a number, not a feeling: how many questions per module you will spend zero solving time on. Roughly 3-5 per module if you are targeting ~600 in a section, 1-2 if you are targeting 750+. Then honor it — the point of the budget is that it stops you from spending three minutes discovering the question was unwinnable.
